title: Aston Villa Closing In On £25m Goalkeeper: Right Move For Emery?
description: Aston Villa are pushing hard to lock down SC Freiburg shot-stopper Noah Atubolu, and negotiations have moved into advanced territory. German outlets, backed up by sources in England, suggest the 23-ye...
fullText:
Aston Villa are pushing hard to lock down SC Freiburg shot-stopper Noah Atubolu, and negotiations have moved into advanced territory. German outlets, backed up by sources in England, suggest the 23-year-old could be packing his bags before the current transfer window shuts. Freiburg certainly seem to think so. They have already snagged Mio Backhaus to take over the gloves, a classic piece of proactive business from a club that rarely signs replacements without a firm reason.

Unai Emery wants real competition and dependable cover for Emi Martinez, and Atubolu fits the brief on paper. Championship interest from Hull City and Coventry City was swiftly knocked back by the player, who wants a proper top-flight setup. Talks with heavyweights like Juventus, AC Milan, and Newcastle have cooled off completely, leaving Villa in pole position.

Freiburg want somewhere between €25m and €30m for their man, which translates to roughly £21m to £26m. Money aside, the player’s camp has made it crystal clear that he will not jump at just any offer. He needs to be convinced by the project.

Looking back at the 2025/26 Bundesliga campaign, Atubolu was an absolute fixture for Freiburg. He racked up 3,060 minutes across all 34 league fixtures, registering six clean sheets and holding a save rate around 63.92%. FotMob pegged his average performance rating at 6.83. He got plenty of continental mileage too, making 15 starts in the Europa League and collecting five clean sheets along the way. Ironically, that run included a 3-0 defeat against Villa in the final back in May.

ISTANBUL, TURKEY – MAY 20: Noah Atubolu of Sport-Club Freiburg looks on during the UEFA Europa League Final 2026 match between SC Freiburg and Aston Villa FC at Besiktas Park on May 20, 2026 in Istanbul, Turkey. (Photo by Maja Hitij/Getty Images)

On paper, this looks like a decent bit of squad planning, but everything hangs on how Emery handles the dynamic once Atubolu walks through the door. Emi Martinez is 32 and remains the undisputed first-choice keeper in the Midlands when fit. He is not stepping aside anytime soon. That leaves a massive question mark over whether Atubolu is actually prepared to sit on the bench week in, week out. Rejecting Championship moves shows plenty of ambition, but riding the bench in the Premier League can turn sour quickly if expectations do not match reality.

The numbers from Germany tell a mixed story. A 63.92% save efficiency across the campaign is solid enough, yet it hardly screams dominant. Freiburg ended up in mid-table, and dropping up to €30m on a backup keeper who might only feature in ten domestic games a year feels expensive.

Then again, managers see things the rest of us miss. If there are underlying concerns about Martinez’s long-term fitness, dropping serious cash on a proven 23-year-old makes financial and tactical sense. Atubolu comes off his line quickly, plays comfortably with the ball at his feet, and already possesses high-level European experience. If Emery views him as the long-term successor rather than an expensive benchwarmer, the fee becomes much easier to digest. Villa just need to ensure the player fully understands his immediate role, because ambition without game time usually brings friction.

title: Tony Romo, NFL broadcaster, arrested on suspicion of OWI in Milwaukee
description: Ex-NFL star and current broadcaster Tony Romo, in the Milwaukee area to compete in the State Amateur golf event, was arrested on suspicion of OWI.
fullText:
Tony Romo, the NFL broadcaster and former NFL quarterback from Burlington, was arrested in Milwaukee on suspicion of operating a vehicle while intoxicated on July 23.

Romo was pulled over driving southbound on Interstate 43 in Milwaukee shortly after 6 p.m. and performed poorly on a field sobriety test, according to the Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office. A first offense for OWI traditionally carries a fine in Wisconsin; the Milwaukee County report gives him a court date of Sept. 21.

Romo was in town participating in the Wisconsin Amateur Championship golf event in West Bend that finished earlier in the day.

Romo, an avid golfer who appears regularly in the state amateur event, has been serving as color commentator for "NFL on CBS" games since 2017 and is one of the more prominent voices in televised sports.

Before that, his 13-year NFL career, spent entirely with the Dallas Cowboys, included four Pro Bowl seasons and made him one of the great undrafted success stories.

Romo played college football at Eastern Illinois following his time at Burlington High School. He still lives in Dallas.

title: Trump stans Sophie Cunningham for trans athletes comment, and he's not alone
description: The White House joins Stephen A. Smith, Martina Navratilova and the anti-trans internet in applauding the WNBA star for saying she wants "to protect young girls in a locker room" from "biological men."
fullText:
After WNBA player Sophie Cunningam made it clear to reporters where she stands on the issue of transgender athletes — following one paragraph in a nearly 5,000 word profile by ESPN — the floodgates of support poured open, with praise from the president of the United States to everyday Americans who feel as she does: "I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men.”

Sports and political pundit Stephen A. Smith said Cunningham “is a thousand percent right” on his SiriusXM Radio show Thursday, echoing transphobic talking points about trans athletes and ignoring the scientific evidence about whether trans women and girls have an advantage in sports.

“What if an NBA player decided to transition to playing in the WNBA?” Smith asked. “How elite would they be? How great would they be? We gotta put stuff in its proper perspective and call it like it is.”

Smith also said he supports establishing separate leagues for trans athletes, apparently unaware that something called the Negro League did something similar to Black professional baseball players until finally being disbanded in 1962.

Trump administration press secretary Karoline Leavitt told the Washington Post and other reporters at the White House Thursday that President Donald Trump is personally “following” coverage of Cunningham’s remarks and has strong feelings about the issue.

“We want to protect women and girls,” Leavitt said, adding that Cunningham was speaking the “truth” about transgender female athletes. Leavitt was backed up by a post on X from the U.S. Department of Education, adding a crown atop Cunningham's head.

“And the backlash she is receiving from Democrats and left-wing figures across the country is astonishing,” Leavitt added.

She's referring to what Out reported, that Cunningham's transphobic dog-whistles, from loaded words like "protect" to "biological men," drew an immediate backlash from WNBA fans, sports writers, and athletes alike, all speaking out against Cunningham's remarks.

That backlash led a half-dozen reporters to confront the athlete Wednesday before she led the Indiana Fever in a blowout win over the Connecticut Sun.

“I think I said what I said,” Cunningham told the gaggle of reporters. “I think it’s kind of common sense. And I think I’ll always believe in that. I think it’s really important to protect children. And that’s little girls who are also involved in that category. And so I stand on what I said, and I always believe that.”

Cunningham was also asked if she's interested in a career in politics after she hangs up her hoops shoes.

“I don’t know. I’m not a very political person,” she said. “But I do have beliefs. I have morals, and I’ll always stand on those and be true to who I am. And I think people are going to take it how they want to take it, but I’ve never even really said anything about that. And so, when it comes just to protecting young girls in sport and women in sport, I feel very strongly about that. I think that’s why you have Title IX. That’s why you have some of the greats in women’s sports. If Title IX and women’s sports weren’t protected, then you wouldn’t hear about any type of women in sports. And so I think in the future it’s just really important to protect.”

When asked if she has any animus for trans people, Cunningham denied it, and repeated what she told ESPN, that she has "never once said I hated the trans community."

“Like I said, I extend love, and I don’t dislike anyone,” she began. “I think there is room for absolutely everyone here, and I think there’s room to love everyone. I truly think when you get people in the same room, and you have conversations, you actually have a lot in common with a lot of people. And so I’m there to love, but I’m also there to love biological women. And I think that there are rights that need to be protected. And like I said, I’m going to stand true to that. I’ll never falter in my beliefs in that. But I have never once said I hated the trans community. Like I said, I think there’s space for everyone.”

Not surprisingly, former tennis star Martina Navratilova — known for her anti-trans remarks — agreed with Cunningham's remarks and shared it in a post on X with her 480K followers, adding two applause emojis and one fistbump emoji.

And that side of the internet jumped on the bandwagon.

But not everyone is cheering for Cunningham.

This article originally appeared on Out: Trump stans Sophie Cunningham for trans athletes comment, and he's not alone

title: Brendan Carr Says ABC's Refusal To Air a Trump Speech Could Affect Renewal of Its Broadcast Licenses
description: The FCC chairman thinks the "public interest" standard is a license to interfere with freedom of the press.
fullText:
Last week, President Donald Trump said ABC and NBC should lose their broadcast licenses because they had dissed him by declining to air his speech about election security. On Wednesday, Brendan Carr, the Trump-appointed chairman of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), suggested he is sympathetic to that view, saying ABC's news-coverage decision will figure in the FCC's ongoing review of the broadcast licenses held by Disney, which owns ABC and its TV stations in eight cities.

Carr's comments reinforce the point that his understanding of the "public interest" that broadcasters are legally obligated to serve is indistinguishable from Trump's personal interests. The idea that the FCC should punish news organizations for exercising their editorial judgment in a way that offends the president is plainly inconsistent with the press freedom guaranteed by the First Amendment. But as Carr sees it, his agency has the authority to restrict that freedom in service of his boss's petty vendettas.

Trump's 24-minute speech, which he delivered from the East Room of the White House on Thursday night, was ostensibly about the need to ensure "fair and honest elections." But before broaching that topic, Trump bragged about his supposed accomplishments for several minutes. And when he got around to discussing election security, he made several dubious statements, including allegations that "members of the deep state" had "worked to actively suppress" information about a "colossal security breach," that they had "blatantly lied" about "the security of our election infrastructure," and that "our elections were left vulnerable to being rigged and stolen."

Although Trump did not explicitly reiterate his long-debunked claim that Joe Biden relied on such chicanery to steal the 2020 presidential election, he described a "plot" to "continue this fraud"—a criminal conspiracy that he said included ABC and NBC. The networks' complicity was clear, he said, from the fact that they did not provide live coverage of his speech "because they know how corrupt our system is, and they don't want to reveal it." He added that "fraud like this should mean a revocation of their licenses."

An FCC chairman who was actually devoted to defending the First Amendment, as Carr claims to be, would have rejected that suggestion out of hand. Although such defiance might seem inconceivable now that Trump has surrounded himself with toadies eager to do his bidding, it happened during his first term, when FCC Chairman Ajit Pai made it clear that he would not act as Trump's hatchet man.

"Network news has become so partisan, distorted and fake that licenses must be challenged and, if appropriate, revoked," Trump declared in October 2017. Pai disagreed in no uncertain terms. "I believe in the First Amendment," he said. "The FCC under my leadership will stand for the First Amendment, and under the law the FCC does not have the authority to revoke a license of a broadcast station based on the content of a particular newscast."

That was then. On Wednesday, Carr made it clear that he does not share Pai's commitment to the First Amendment.

"You were asked before the president's speech last week if carrying this speech is part of a broadcaster's public interest obligations, and you didn't say one way or another," Communications Daily Associate Editor Monty Taloe noted during an FCC press conference. "Then, during the speech, the president said ABC and NBC should lose their licenses for not carrying it. Does that mean carrying those [presidential] speeches is part of a broadcaster's public interest obligation?"

Carr's response: "When you have the president of the United States standing inside the White House delivering an important speech, I think that's something that broadcasters should be carrying. And so, obviously, this is an issue. There have been lots of concerns raised, including by members of Congress, about whether broadcasters and their decisions there comply with [the] public interest. With respect to Disney [and] ABC in particular, we have an open proceeding right now on whether they've been operating in the public interest, and I'm sure that there are going to be points raised in that proceeding that relate to Disney's decision there."

Deadline Political Editor Ted Johnson asked Carr to clarify whether he was saying that ABC's decision not to air the speech "could be held against Disney" because "in your eyes, they're not fulfilling their public interest obligation." Broadcasters "should be doing that," Carr reiterated. "Any time a broadcaster is not operating in the public interest, that raises significant concerns," he said, and "yes, the FCC is going to hold people accountable to their public interest obligations. "

Johnson noted that the networks say, "Hey, we have made this call before under President Biden, under President Obama, where we did not carry each and every one of their presidential addresses when the White House requested it." Carr was unfazed. "As a general matter," he said, "when the president speaks from the White House on a significant matter, I think that's something that broadcasters should be allowing their viewers to get access to. So whether it happened before or not, I can't speak to that."

Carr's suggestion that NBC and ABC somehow prevented Americans interested in Trump's speech from seeing it is plainly silly. Fox News and Fox broadcast stations carried the speech live in its entirety, and so did various streaming services and online platforms, including ABC News Live, NBC News NOW, CNN.com, the PBS and Associated Press YouTube channels, and the White House's website and social media accounts. CBS and MSNBC aired excerpts of the speech, albeit accompanied by commentary and fact-checking.

Trump's position is that NBC and ABC nevertheless committed an unpardonable sin, worthy of a death sentence for their network-owned stations, by declining to give Americans a couple of other options for watching his speech. And Carr clearly agrees that broadcasting Trump's speech was part of the networks' "public interest" obligations. Never mind that TV networks historically have exercised their journalistic judgment in deciding which presidential speeches to air. While that might have been acceptable when Democrats such as Biden and Obama occupied the White House, it is intolerable under Trump, who views personal slights as a justification for government retaliation.

Carr initiated the "open proceeding" that he mentioned during his press conference in April, when he informed Disney and ABC that the FCC was "calling in Disney's ABC licenses for early renewal" years before they otherwise would have been subject to review. Carr said the FCC was investigating ABC and Disney for "possible violations of the Communications Act of 1934 and the FCC's rules, including the agency's prohibition on unlawful discrimination."

Carr was referring to the FCC's concerns about "Disney's DEI practices." But even at the outset, he signaled a broader inquiry, encompassing "possible violations of the Communications Act of 1934," which provides the main legal authority for requiring broadcasters to serve "the public interest." And as Carr's take on presidential speeches illustrates, he interprets that standard broadly enough to justify FCC interference with freedom of the press.

Such government meddling would be clearly unconstitutional in any other medium. But "when it comes to broadcast TV," Carr noted at Wednesday's press conference, "I've always said it's different." Why? Because, Carr avers, "the American people have subsidized broadcasters to the tune of billions of dollars by providing free access to the nation's airwaves."

In reality, companies like Disney do not have "free access to the nation's airwaves," because broadcast licenses figure in the price they pay when they acquire TV and radio stations. But Carr thinks this fiction empowers him to penalize news outlets for making decisions that Trump does not like.

The Supreme Court's 1969 rationale for limiting the First Amendment rights of broadcasters, which hinged on "the scarcity of radio frequencies," likewise never made much sense. It makes even less sense today given the plethora of media options available to Americans—the reason Carr's avowed concern about "access to" Trump's speech is so implausible.

Even taking for granted the arbitrary distinction between broadcast content and speech in all other media, it has never before been understood to justify the sort of heavy-handed intervention that Carr thinks the "public interest" standard demands. "The agency is prohibited by law from engaging in censorship or infringing on First Amendment rights of the press," the FCC itself says. "Those protected rights include, but are not limited to, a broadcaster's selection and presentation of news or commentary."

When a TV network decides whether to offer live, unexpurgated coverage of a president's speech, it is clearly engaging in the "selection and presentation of news." Yet Carr thinks such decisions "obviously" raise "an issue" as to "whether broadcasters and their decisions there comply with public interest," which is the standard that the FCC applies when it decides whether to renew licenses.

During the same press conference, Anna Gomez, the lone Democratic member of the FCC, took a different view. "It is not for the FCC to tell broadcasters how to make their editorial decisions or what content to place on their networks or their local broadcast stations," she said. "They have a First Amendment right to make those decisions….If we tell them they can't broadcast something, that's censorship, and it's compelled speech if we tell them they have to do so."

Officially, the FCC recognizes its constitutional and statutory obligation to refrain from such meddling. "The limitations on the FCC's power to restrict or ban speech begin with the First Amendment," it notes. And under the Communications Act, "no regulation or condition shall be promulgated or fixed by the Commission which shall interfere with the right of free speech by means of radio communication."

In light of "these legal mandates," the commission says, "the FCC has long held that 'the public interest is best served by permitting free expression of views.' Rather than suppress speech, communications law and policy seeks to encourage responsive 'counter-speech' from others. Following this principle ensures that the most diverse and opposing opinions will be expressed, even though some views or expressions may be highly offensive."

Carr did not seem to be following that policy when he threatened broadcasters with fines and license revocation if they failed to punish late-night comedian Jimmy Kimmel for comments that offended Carr and the president. In that case, ABC and its affiliates immediately sought to placate Carr by suspending Kimmel's show—precisely the punishment that Carr had recommended. What happened to tolerating "diverse and opposing opinions" even when they "may be highly offensive"?

Given Carr's manifest disregard for freedom of speech, he might want to delete the FCC's online assurances that it will comply with the limits imposed by the First Amendment and the Communications Act. "I continue to say that this vague public interest standard is being used just to punish speech that this administration doesn't like and to reward speech that it does like," Gomez said on Wednesday. "That's inappropriate, and it's contrary to the law and to the Constitution."

Carr is undaunted by such objections. "We're going to hold all broadcasters to [meeting their] public interest obligations, and we're always looking to make sure that they're doing exactly that," he said. "And I think there's more work for us on this issue ahead."

The post Brendan Carr Says ABC's Refusal To Air a Trump Speech Could Affect Renewal of Its Broadcast Licenses appeared first on Reason.com.

title: Meet SLB: The $70 billion oil services giant poised to cash in on AI data centers and the post-Strait of Hormuz oil exploration boom
description: For nearly a century, SLB has helped energy companies find hard-to-reach reserves. Now the global energy realignment is giving the French-Texan company a fresh growth story.
fullText:
In 1912, the French physicist Conrad Schlumberger could be found kneeling on the ground of his family's estate in Normandy, strategically placing wired electrodes in the soil. He was performing conductivity tests to detect the buried ruins of a medieval abbey destroyed there during the French Revolution. But the experiment had a broader purpose: proving that electric instruments could be used to reveal and map underground structures from the surface. Schlumberger's approach worked, and it turned out to be a remarkably effective tool for a more lucrative enterprise: finding oil.

Conrad and his brother Marcel Schlumberger went on to create the first well logs—using electric cables for subsurface readings, producing outputs that resembled EKG heart monitor readings. The method became the backbone of modern geophysical prospecting, and supercharged the growth of a burgeoning oil and gas exploration industry worldwide. In 1926 the brothers founded the Société de Prospection Électrique (Electric Prospecting Co.). That company—eventually Schlumberger and now SLB—rapidly expanded into Venezuela, the United States, and the Soviet Union. By the end of the 1930s, Schlumberger had moved into the Middle East, more than 20 years before the formation of OPEC.

Over a century of upheaval and industrial reinvention, SLB has grown into the largest oilfield services and energy technology company in the world. Known in the industry as "Big Blue" for its signature blue uniforms, it has remained in all those key locations, and expanded to another 100 countries.

Now, as the Middle East's oil and gas sector rebounds from the biggest energy supply shock in modern history—the monthslong closure of the Strait of Hormuz—and Venezuela rebuilds its energy infrastructure, SLB is ideally positioned to profit from this growth in its next century.

In the energy services industry, which does all the grunt work for oil producers—drilling, fracking, and, increasingly, digital and AI-driven automation services—SLB is larger than its better-known American rivals, Halliburton and Baker Hughes. With 109,000 workers worldwide, SLB employs more people than ExxonMobil and Chevron combined.

In Venezuela, SLB and Chevron—two companies that never left the country even after the Hugo Chávez regime expropriated oil assets—will work with state-owned PDVSA to reinvigorate the world's largest proven oil reserves. In the Middle East, SLB partners with Saudi Aramco, the United Arab Emirates' ADNOC, Kuwait Petroleum, and others.

title: Trump to impose 'forced labor' duties on Friday as temporary 10% US tariffs expire
description: The Trump administration on Friday will impose new tariffs of 10% and 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners, including the European Union, over allegations of lax
fullText:
July 23 (Reuters) - The Trump administration on Friday will impose new tariffs of 10% and 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners, including the European Union, over allegations of lax enforcement of forced labor bans, just as a temporary 10% global tariff expires.

The move is the White House's latest effort to restore President Donald Trump's campaign vision of a near-global tariff after ‌the U.S. Supreme Court in February struck down his "reciprocal" duties of 10% to 50% imposed last year under a national emergencies law to try to shrink the U.S. trade deficit.

The new tariffs, announced ‌on Thursday in a Federal Register notice, will cover 99.4% of U.S. imports, but include numerous product exemptions, such as oil and gas, fertilizer and certain food items.

Imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, the new duties allow the administration to maintain a tariff floor ​on virtually all U.S. imports despite the Supreme Court setback. The tariffs are also likely to face less legal risk than those struck down in February, as Section 301 has survived prior court challenges.

Trump responded to the February Supreme Court ruling by imposing a temporary 10% tariff for 150 days that expires at 12:01 a.m. EDT on Friday (0401 GMT). The new duties will take effect at that exact same moment, with goods in transit exempted until 12:01 a.m. EDT on July 28.

"The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it. It's well past time for our trading partners to do the same," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement. "Today's action will begin ‌to correct what is both a human rights abuse and distortive trade practice ⁠to improve the welfare of workers everywhere."

Greer has previously pledged that for countries that have reached trade deals with Washington capping U.S. tariff rates, the new forced labor duties would not push them above those caps.

Under the final determination, the U.S. will impose a 10% duty on goods of Argentina, Bangladesh, Britain, Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India, ⁠Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago.

The European Union, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland were assigned rates that, combined with pre-existing most-favored-nation tariff rates, would total 10% or 12.5%.

The other 38 countries were assigned a 12.5% rate. These include China, accused by the U.S. of detaining Uyghur minorities in work camps, which Beijing denies.

title: Tens of thousands evacuated from French tourist spot and near Madrid as wildfires spread
description: The fire has raged in the region for several days with officials now ordering the evacuation of the entire Cap Ferret peninsula.
fullText:
Watch: Wildfires rage across France and Spain

French authorities have ordered the evacuation of the entirety of the Cap Ferret peninsula on the south-west coast, with hundreds of people escaping by boat.

Tens of thousands of people are being evacuated from the tourist spot west of Bordeaux, as firefighters continue to battle what the local prefect described as an "XXL fire" in the Gironde region.

The fires, which began on Tuesday, have burned for days, with officials saying 10,000 hectares (almost 25,000 acres) had been consumed by flames.

Meanwhile, Spain's government has declared a national emergency after wildfires burnt out of control in several areas close to the capital Madrid, prompting the evacuation of more than 19,000 people.

Responding to the spread of fires, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, Madrid's regional president, said it was: "The worst fire in the history of the region."

Speaking at an emergency command post in the southwestern municipality of Cenicientos, she said the area was facing a "perfect storm" with high temperatures, relentless wind and several fire fronts merging.

"The situation is completely unusual and catastrophic," she said, adding that the priority was saving lives.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez spoke of a "dramatic situation" and urged people to take great care. Three fires were burning west of Madrid, at Villa del Prado and San Martín de Valdeiglesias.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 40,000 people had either been or were in the process of being evacuated from the Cap Ferret peninsula, which has the Atlantic on one side and the Bay of Arcachon on the other.

Local prefect Sophie Brocas said 53 homes had been lost as well as a campsite, but that 2,000 houses had been saved.

A local councillor said 2,000 evacuees from the peninsula had already arrived by boat in the port of Arcachon on the south side of the bay.

Fire and rescue chief Marc Vermeulen said the wildfire had spread rapidly at the end of Thursday and into the early hours of Friday. Authorities then took the decision on Friday morning to begin the evacuation of the town of Arès, which lies south-east of Lège-Cap Ferret on the Bay of Arcachon.

Vermeulen compared the fires overnight to those in 2022 - explaining the area is in a more severe state of drought now.

While in 2022, fires were "exploding" at the end of the day and the nights were favourable for firefighting, in the current fires they are exploding during the night at midnight or 01:00.

"When I say explosion, it means that for several hours, we had propagation speeds on the order of 800 to 1,000 hectares burned per hour, in the context of a suburban area."

Further down the Atlantic coast, around the town of Biscarrosse in France's Landes region, another major fire that began on Thursday afternoon has prompted the evacuations of more than 23,000 people.

About 18,000 people in Biscarrosse and 5,000 in Parentis-en-Born had to leave their homes, campsites, a nursing home and a summer camp.

Landes prefect Gilles Clavreul said the fire around Biscarrosse was not going to be out by the end of Friday, with winds of up to 50km/h (31mph) and temperatures of 36-37C.

He added that 105 homes and other buildings had so far been identified as either partially or completely destroyed by the flames.

No further casualties have been reported overnight in south-west France, although two firefighters died on Tuesday while tackling a blaze near Bordeaux airport.

French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday night the wildfire situation in the country was "very tense" - especially in the Gironde region.

The European Union has sent three planes and two helicopters to help the French fire effort, and another four planes to Spain.

Headmaster David Morton, 53, from Gloucester in southwest England had been on holiday with his wife and sons when they received an emergency alert via text overnight on Thursday instructing them to evacuate.

The family were staying in a house in Petit Piquey, along the peninsula, and were woken up at 03:00 local time (01:00 GMT) by an alert on the property's landline.

"Everyone was driving with their lights on, driving very slowly – there was lots of fire service people, ambulances, police on the other side of the road controlling things and we could see several fires in the distance as we drove," he told the BBC.

"It's different from seeing it on the television… seeing it blazing out of control despite hundreds and hundreds of firemen and women helping."

Olivia Jarratt, 44, was evacuated from Truc Vert campsite on the peninsula with her husband and two children in the early hours of Friday morning.

Her daughter was woken with sirens and the family left their tent, camping gear and bikes behind as they made the drive to Bordeaux.

"At first, we dismissed it, and thought she was having a nightmare, but we realised it was all going on, and everyone was packing in a panic. There's only one road off the peninsula, so people were trying to be as quick as possible.

"There was a loudspeaker with the sirens, but obviously that was in French, and with everything, we couldn't understand what was happening."

The Cap Ferret peninsula has a year-round population of just under 8,000 but that can swell by 10 times that number in peak season.

Around 20,000 people within the Gironde region had been evacuated on Thursday many of whom were visitors to campsites on the peninsula.

"This is a tourist disaster that we are experiencing once again," Franck Chaumès, president of the Gironde branch of the Union of Hotel Trades and Industries, told FranceInfo.

He added that the union was working to secure financial aid and "potentially offer some rooms to displaced residents".

In Spain, Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska declared a national emergency as fires burned at Villa del Prado and San Martín de Valdeiglesias in the Madrid region and at Burgohondo in Ávila.

Local emergency services said on Friday afternoon that the Madrid fires had merged, while more than 19,000 people had been evacuated from their homes in three towns west of the capital.

The mayor of El Tiemblo, one of the affected areas in Ávila, said the fire had spread from Navaluenga to the Iruelas Valley - a distance of about 20km (12 miles) - in less than half an hour. "It was horrific," Arturo Varas González told laSexta.

"The smoke was incredibly thick. You couldn't breathe," Jose Cobos, who escaped with his wife and three dogs, told Antena 3.

Residents of Chapinería, Navas del Rey, and Colmenar del Arroyo have received Es-Alert messages to leave.

Pedro Sánchez said earlier in the day that forest fires were "ravaging thousands of hectares" and affecting numerous communities.

An update on Friday morning had described the two fires that have now joined as being "out of control".

Grande-Marlaska said 9,000 hectares (around 22,200 acres) had burned in Ávila, and 3,000 in Madrid.

It followed earlier evacuations from Aldea del Fresno and other parts of the region.

Europe is the fastest-warming continent, heating at more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service. That rapid rise in temperatures is making its summers hotter and, particularly in the south, drier.

The hotter, drier conditions leave soils, trees and other vegetation with less moisture, creating the fuel in which wildfires can take hold. A spark is still needed - most often from human activity, usually accidental but sometimes deliberate, or from lightning.

Once a fire starts, extreme heat, dry vegetation and strong winds can help it spread faster, burn more intensely and become much harder to control.

How forests and landscapes are managed also matters: accumulated vegetation and abandoned land can provide more fuel for fires. But the European Environment Agency has said "climate change has increased forest fire risk across Europe", with the greatest danger expected in southern Europe.

Additional reporting by BBC climate editor Justin Rowlatt and Alex Akhurst

title: I’ve been gaming for 40 years. Here are the best chairs in the UK for comfort, support and serious play
description:
Whether you’re on PC or a console, level up your setup with our gaming expert’s pick of the best chairs
• The best games of 2026 so far
Comfort is crucial to the gaming experience. It’s hard to focus on blasting aliens or taking Stoke to the Champions League final if your bum has gone to sleep because you’ve been sitting on an old chair for three hours. We’re spending more time playing games than ever before, so good posture matters. If you have set up a dedicated gaming space, then a rickety seat just won’t cut it.
From luxurious ergonomic thrones to cheap-and-cheerful bucket seats, the options available are bewildering.
fullText:
Whether you’re on PC or a console, level up your setup with our gaming expert’s pick of the best chairs

Comfort is crucial to the gaming experience. It’s hard to focus on blasting aliens or taking Stoke to the Champions League final if your bum has gone to sleep because you’ve been sitting on an old chair for three hours. We’re spending more time playing games than ever before, so good posture matters. If you have set up a dedicated gaming space, then a rickety seat just won’t cut it.

From luxurious ergonomic thrones to cheap-and-cheerful bucket seats, the options available are bewildering. So I set out on an epic quest: to find the most comfortable, durable and stylish gaming chairs. Here’s what I discovered.

Best gaming chair overall:

 Secretlab Titan Evo

Best budget gaming chair:

 ThunderX3 Solo 360

Best mid-range gaming chair:

 ThunderX3 Core

Best for combining gaming and working:

 Herman Miller x Logitech G Embody

Best for improving posture:

 Anthros the Chair

I have been playing video games for 40 years (gulp), and writing about them for my entire career as a journalist. I spend most of my waking hours sitting with a joypad in hand, and as a sufferer of lower back pain too (gee, I wonder why?), being comfortable while I’m “working” is vital. I’m also a veteran reviewer of gaming technology, including joypads, monitors, keyboards and headsets. In short, I know what people need from their games hardware.

I’m paid to sit and play video games all day (and often into the night), so that’s exactly what I did to test the chairs here. I started by noting how easy or challenging they were to assemble, how sturdy they felt and their level of adjustability. I also judged how cool they looked as part of my gaming setup.

I tested 10 gaming chairs over five days each, spending up to four hours a day sitting on them, playing a variety of games, from restful puzzlers to intense shooters and complex flight sims. I also sought the opinions of my sons, who are also keen gamers, and my wife – who isn’t at all interested in games, but who works from home, so was able to assess each model as an occasional office chair.

Once the testing process was finished, the chairs were donated to the video games accessibility charity, SpecialEffect, so that other people will get to enjoy them while blasting noobs in Fortnite.

Secretlab is a cool upmarket brand, beloved of many game streamers. Inside the box, the Titan Evo was packaged so neatly and stylishly, it felt as if I was unwrapping a giant iPhone. Although there are a lot of parts, I assembled it in less than 20 minutes, thanks to the poster-sized quick-start guide. My sample came in a sleek, matt-black leatherette finish, but there’s also a fabric version, plus a range of tasteful colours and designs to choose from. It comes in three sizes; I chose the XL because I like a LOT of space.

Why we love it
As a natural contrarian I wanted to dislike this much-hyped chair, but I couldn’t. The Titan is solid, beautiful and futuristic, looking like it’s been removed from the bridge of some extraordinarily luscious starship. The controls for the armrests and recline functions are well placed, with adjustments available to tweak the curvature and height of the lumbar support. The seat is capacious enough for lounging, and the leatherette is soft to the touch.

My wife found the seat too firm, and while I agreed initially, after a few days I realised it was helping me stay alert over long gaming sessions. Now, everything else feels like sitting on a marshmallow. (As an aside, I have also tried the new Evo NanoGen edition, which you may find offers a bit more give.)

The Titan Evo is neither cheap nor as ergonomically advanced as the Herman Miller or Anthros, yet it was the chair I looked forward to sitting in and really enjoyed using.

It’s a shame that … the warranty is only three years. You can extend it to five years by posting a photo of your chair on social media, but I dislike the idea of customer support being incentivised in this way.

Dimensions (XL version): 78 x 70 x 145cm (WDH)
Seat depth and height: 50cm, 46-55.5cm
Adjustments: lumbar support, armrests, recline, tilt lock
Brand’s sustainability claims: 90% of packaging is recycled paper content. Chair has modular design: if a component wears out over time, it can be replaced

A lot of so-called “ergonomic” gaming chairs at the sub-£200 price point are made with squeaky faux leather, plastic parts and sport brash designs – but not the Solo 360. Its slim build and muted grey and black colour options look sophisticated and are backed up with a solid steel construction. There are four variations – Racer, Mesh, Modern and the Loft Air Light version I tested – all in different materials.

Why we love it 
As well as being quick and easy to assemble, I was surprised by how comfortable the Solo 360 is, even over long periods – a view shared by my wife. The armrests are adjustable for both height and angle, and I welcomed the synchronous tilt, which reclines the back and the seat together for a laid-back feel, while your feet stay firmly on the ground. For less than £200, the ThunderX3 is a chair you can use for gaming, working and – possibly – sleeping.

It’s a shame that … the seat is rather low, and although the back is curved for lumbar support, the position wasn’t suitable for someone of my height (I’m 6ft 3in). However, this all makes it a good choice for shorter gamers.

Dimensions: 72-86 x 70 x 127-140cm (WDH) 
Seat depth and height: 48cm, 45-53cm
Adjustments: seat height, tilt, armrests, backrest resistance
Brand’s sustainability claims: armrests and wheels made of plastic contain 30% recycled materials. Metal products use approximately 70% recycled materials. Most components apart from leather, fabric and foam are recyclable. Spare parts available

Widely acclaimed by the gaming press, the ThunderX3 Core is a chunky, comfortable chair with a large winged back that envelops you. The chair offers several adjustability options, including the same synchronous tilt feature as the Solo, so the backrest and seat move together for ultimate comfort. I also appreciated the ability to slope the seat downwards, to really lean into the action yet take the pressure off the backs of my knees after hours of play.

Why we love it
The fabric version of the seat has the smoothest upholstery of all the chairs here – a really lovely soft feel. It also features a lumbar panel on the rear that moves with you as you lean from side to side, for excellent support while playing shooters and driving sims, for example. I didn’t like this feature as much for working, though.

It’s a shame that … although it’s easy to assemble, the heads of its hex screws are way too shallow and vulnerable to stripping. Also, the adjustment controls are awkwardly positioned and the armrests rattle a bit.

Dimensions: 70 x 70 x 129-139cm (WDH) 
Seat depth and height: 45-50cm, 46-56cm 
Adjustments: height, tilt, armrests
Brand’s sustainability claims: see ThunderX3 Solo 360 above

The Embody is Herman Miller’s premium gaming chair – and it shows. Whether you’re leaning into the screen or tilting back for a chilled session, its strong aluminium frame and high-end fabrics, including heat-dissipating composite particles, combine to keep you comfortable and cool. Available in a range of understated colours to suit more mature tastes, it arrives fully assembled – I was seated and playing Arc Raiders within 10 minutes of it being delivered.

Why we love it
The Embody is an impressively svelte chair. It has a narrow silhouette and a lower back than many of its competitors; there’s no headrest, nor does it offer some of the more intricate adjustments, such as 4D armrests or precise lumbar control. But it doesn’t need to – its clean, precise, ergonomic design gently encourages you to sit comfortably and correctly without you even realising.

There are levers allowing you to tilt fully, extend the seat depth or alter the back to fit your spine, but I didn’t have to spend ages getting everything right. The armrests are perfectly placed, the seat allows plenty of movement, and my spine felt cushioned, even when I spent all day in it – which made it great for work, too.

It’s a shame that … it’s expensive – but worth the money, if you’ll be using it for hours daily and it’s doubling as a home office chair. It comes with an impressive 12-year warranty, and when it does finally give up, the company claims it is up to 96% recyclable.

Dimensions: 74.9 x 38.1-45.7 x 106.7-114.3cm (WDH) 
Seat depth and height: 38.1-45.7cm; 43.2-55.9cm
Adjustments: seat height, seat depth, tilt and back fit, armrest height and width
Brand’s sustainability claims: corporate sustainability programme. Worn parts replaced free under warranty (outside that, UK customers are pointed to third-party suppliers). Made from 44% recycled materials. Chair is up to 96% recyclable at end of life

The Anthros is a serious piece of ergonomic equipment with intricately adjustable, well-placed controls for tilt, height and back support. Designed to stabilise your pelvis in order to alleviate back pain, its creators are as obsessed with posture as an overbearing Victorian governess – but in a good way. Indeed, the team used to design wheelchairs, so they know about ensuring long-term comfort.

Customers are even offered a complimentary video session with an expert in order to calibrate it properly. The chair frame comes in black or white, with a range of colours, textures and designs available for the rear of the backrest. It ships in two sections, so there’s little assembly.

Why we love it
As with the Herman Miller and Secretlab models, the Anthros offers a firm sit, with just the right amount of padding to keep glutes and upper thighs comfy. The back is made of two sections, one providing pelvis support, and the other gently cushioning your upper back – this part actually moves with you slightly as you lean left or right, which ensures you’re always in optimum contact with the chair. The decompress mode lets you tilt back and relax while still maintaining a healthy position.

After using it for a couple of weeks, I felt I was much better at sitting properly and experienced less of my usual pain when getting up. Whether I was bolt upright for hours writing articles, or wildly slamming about playing Call of Duty, it quite literally had my back.

It’s a shame that … it’s already pricey, but with US-only distribution pushing UK shipping costs to $307.71 (about £230) right now, it’s a significant investment. However, if you struggle with back pain, it’s excellent as a gaming and office chair.

Dimensions: 66 x 67 x 101.9-110.9cm (WDH)
Seat depth and height: 38.7-46.6cm, 48-59cm
Adjustments: tilt, seat height, upper and lower back
Brand’s sustainability claims: most parts are potentially recyclable (although it may be a struggle due to a lack of processing streams in the UK). Spare parts available. 12-year warranty

The Tempest is clearly aimed at a younger market, with sports car styling and fun LED panels that light up in a variety of colours. It was easy to assemble and feels pretty comfortable to sit in, with thick padding, a wide seat and rudimentary lumbar support. It’s a decent first gaming chair.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the build quality is basic, and there are no adjustment options apart from seat height. I’m not sure how it will hold up with regular use – although the one-year warranty covers replacement parts, and spares can be bought beyond that.

Dimensions: 69 x 67 x 114.5-122.5cm (WDH); seat depth and height: 60cm, 45-53cm; adjustments: height; brand’s sustainability claims: company is FIRA registered and audits factories to ensure best practices. Metal parts can be recycled. Parts can be exchanged for free under one-year warranty or bought outside that period at the manufacturer’s discretion

A bit more expensive than the Tempest, the Corsair comes in fabric and leatherette versions (I tested the fabric version) and has a wide seat designed to let you slob out a little as you play. It also comes with lumbar and neck pillows, and adjustable arms.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the racing car styling is cool, but the construction and materials lack the quality of more expensive models, and some parts were tricky to put together. It’s a decent entry-level gaming chair, but at this price, a dedicated office chair may be a better option for longer sessions and/or back pain sufferers.

Dimensions: 67 x 68 x 124-132cm (WDH); seat depth and height: 50cm, 45-55cm; adjustments: height, recline, armrests; brand’s sustainability claims: corporate sustainability programme. Comes with a two-year manufacturer’s guarantee

Best for: all-round performance

The Legend really does look like a sports car seat, with beautifully stitched faux leather fabric (vegan and sustainably made), a high-winged back, and sleek styling. There’s plenty of range to the tilt, and both the lumbar support and armrests are fully adjustable. I found it comfortable over long periods, so it can happily double as an office chair, plus it’s robust – and the company stocks spare parts, if needed.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I found the seat too shallow (I’m 6ft 3in) and the armrests uncomfortable, no matter how I adjusted them. There are slightly better options at this price point.

Dimensions: 52 x 73 x 132-142cm (WDH); seat depth and height: 48cm, 48-58cm; adjustments: tilt, armrests, lumbar support; brand’s sustainability claims: solvent- and phthalate-free materials and manufactured with low emissions. Metal parts recyclable. Chairs come with a two-year warranty covering parts

Best for: solid, sensible build quality

The Refine is an extremely well-built chair with a minimalist design that would suit the offices of some trendy Gothenburg architecture firm. Everything is easily adjustable, mostly via cool little tabs rather than the usual protruding levers, and the mesh fabric is comfortable and keeps you cool – although my younger son said it felt like sitting in a camping chair. Fractal also offers good after-care support, including spare parts.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the seat is a little shallow for taller users even at full extension, and I had to detach the headrest cushion as it was too invasive. Better as a quality office chair that you use occasionally for gaming, rather than the other way around.

Dimensions: 70 x 70 x 134-146.5cm (WDH); seat depth and height: 45-50.5cm, 49-61cm; adjustments: recline, height, armrests, lumbar support, headrest; brand’s sustainability claims: one more expensive Fractal Refine model uses Alcantara, a material with recycled elements. The company is moving to plastic‑free packaging. Metal sections can be recycled. Five-year warranty on mechanical parts and a three-year warranty on soft parts

If you only play console games for a few hours a week in front of a big TV in the living room, a nice slouchy armchair or even a beanbag is fine. However, if you play games at a desk with a monitor and want to feel comfortable, a decent chair is a good investment, especially for long gaming sessions, or if you also work at the desk from time to time.

It’s all about design purpose. An office chair is intended to support posture and productivity for several hours a day and will probably come with ergonomic features that allow you to fine-tune your sitting experience. A gaming chair is designed primarily for shorter-term comfort because, sadly, you’re unlikely to spend as much time playing games as you are working.

The design tends to focus on fun and immersion, which is why many look as if they’ve been pulled from a sports car or rollercoaster, featuring high-winged backs, headrests, lots of padding, and seats with raised edges. An office chair is usually conservative and unobtrusive; gaming chairs often sport a bolder look, with bright colours and extravagant design touches.

If you’re on a tight budget (£200 or less) and don’t care about flashy looks, an office chair is almost certainly a better choice, as they tend to be more sturdily built and ergonomically designed at this price.

For more, read our guide to the best office chairs

You need a chair that’s right for your size and gaming habits – for good posture, you should be able to plant your feet on the floor with your knees at a 90-degree angle and your upper legs parallel to the floor. If you’re a larger build or move a lot while playing, choose a chair with a wider, deeper seat. If you’re tall or experience back pain, go for an ergonomic model with good lumbar support.

Consider the way you play games. If you use a mouse and keyboard, then armrests are a good idea, but if you use a joypad and hold it close to your lap, they may get in the way of your elbows (unless they can be rotated, as chairs such as the Titan Evo, Anthros, Core and Refine allow). If you like to sit back with your feet up, make sure the chair has a deep tilt angle. If you’ll be working in your chair as well as gaming, consider a model with ergonomic features and more space to move about.

Think about how much time you will spend in the chair and how long you expect it to last. From £180, you can buy a comfortable, solidly built gaming chair that will suit most casual to intermediate gamers; from £350, models offer greater adjustability for posture and lumbar support, and are more likely to be built to last.

For more, read the best PS5 games to play in 2026 and the best of 2026 so far

As a veteran technology journalist, Keith Stuart has spent years testing gaming gadgets from headsets to keyboards to full PC builds, so he knows what gamers need. He also spends a disproportionate amount of time sitting down and so is doubly qualified to put gaming chairs through their paces

title: I'm 55 and have applied to over 300 jobs. I never expected my 32 years of experience to work against me.
description: After being laid off, a 55-year-old communications professional applied to more than 300 jobs. She feels defeated and is lowering her expectations.
fullText:
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Leslie Sonnenklar, a 55-year-old communications and content professional from Phoenix, Arizona. It's been edited for length and clarity.

I was laid off in March 2025, and honestly, the job search since then has been one of the most frustrating and defeating experiences of my life.

As a professional in my mid-50s, I have more than 32 years of experience in the communications industry. I started my career in 1994 as a marketing coordinator, owned my own business for 11 years, and most recently served as the director of content and communications at a marketing agency.

Over the last 14 months, I've applied for over 300 jobs. I've tailored my résumé, written thoughtful cover letters, reached out to hiring managers, met with recruiters, and tried to keep an open mind about positions with titles similar to those I held much earlier in my career.

Many people are nice and say things like, "Oh, I've been there twice" or even three times. I've never been in a situation where I couldn't find a job. It's difficult, and sometimes I feel embarrassed. Still, I have to believe that I'll find something — that it's all a blip —and I'll pick right back up where I left off.

In Still in the Game, Business Insider is chronicling the realities of job hunting in your 50s — from overcoming age bias and navigating career transitions to rebuilding confidence, updating skills, and finding new opportunities in a competitive job market. Read more stories here, and share your own experience here.

LinkedIn will say "over 100 people" have applied to a job — but that could mean 101 or 1,001. It makes me feel like the odds are stacked against me before anyone has even seen my résumé.

I find it hard to believe companies look at my résumé and think I'm not qualified. I make it a point to tailor every résumé with AI to align my experience with what they say they want in the job description. I know I bring value. I bring good judgment, perspective, maturity, creativity, and decades of experience helping organizations strengthen their brand.

I truly want to learn and innovate, and I even taught younger people how to use AI at my last agency. It's been hard to stay optimistic, but I know I have to because I still need to come across as professional, capable, and qualified.

The only conclusion I can come to is that I'm overqualified for a lot of these jobs, or they think that I'm too stuck in my ways because I've been doing this for 32 years. I believe ageism is at play in today's job market. I was even told by recruiters: only include the last 10 years of your job history.

A company can hire someone in their 20s or 30s and pay them less, and mold them. Maybe companies are looking to teach younger employees along the way and pay them less than what they'd pay someone with my experience.

Companies say they're looking for experienced people, but the job descriptions read like they're looking for a unicorn. I've seen roles that want one person to lead strategy, write copy, manage SEO, be an analytics expert, and even handle design. Those aren't the same skill sets, and senior communications professionals shouldn't have to have all of those to prove their value.

In 2025, I was only applying for remote jobs because that's what I ideally want. But after nine months and only a few interviews, I started applying to jobs with companies in the Phoenix area.

I also pivoted away from applying to jobs posted on LinkedIn and started focusing more on jobs where I could find an inside connection or referral. When you're out of work and doing everything you can, even a small introduction can feel like a lifeline.

One of the more frustrating things has been reaching out to people I know — including people I've known for years — and getting no response.

Occasionally, someone has been kind enough to make an introduction to a hiring manager or recruiter, and I've secured a couple of interviews that way, but it hasn't been enough.

This search has been one of the most humbling experiences of my life. I never thought I'd be in this situation. The constant questions from family and friends come from a good place, but every time I have to say, "No, I still haven't found a job," it makes the process feel even more defeating.

I'm not worried about my future retirement, financial plans, or sense of stability yet. I've saved well — I was smart and planned financially, should something like this ever happen.

It does bother me, though, that I want to be prepared when I do retire, and I've spent the last year not contributing to that retirement. I also know that it's just a matter of not finding that right opportunity. I know in my heart that I'll find something.

Do you have a story to share about navigating your career in your 50s? If so, please reach out to the reporter at tmartinelli@businessinsider.com.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Arkansas cop tragically dies saving fiancée's life just hours after proposing
description: An Arkansas police officer proposed to his fiancée hours before drowning in Elk River while rescuing her from the current during a canoeing trip with friends.
fullText:
An Arkansas police officer drowned after entering a river to save his fiancée just hours after proposing to her, according to her mother.

Fred Marsh, 24, of the Rogers Police Department, entered Missouri's Elk River on Saturday to help another swimmer and did not resurface, according to the Missouri State Highway Patrol. His fiancée's mother identified that swimmer as her daughter. Marsh was recovered and pronounced dead Sunday after asking his fiancée, Hailey, to marry him Saturday morning.

"They had been together for three beautiful years, and they had a very beautiful, loving relationship," Sheryl Padgett told KHBS. "Even though legally he was not my son-in-law, he will forever be my son."

The pair, who had been together for three years, were out canoeing with another couple on the river near Noel, Missouri, when Hailey entered the water and began struggling against the current while trying to return to the boat.

'Hero' Mom Dies After Using Last Strength To Save 4-Year-old Son From Florida River

Marsh and a fellow Rogers police officer who was with them then jumped into the water to help her, Padgett said. They were able to move her to safety, but Marsh became distressed and exhausted, went underwater and never resurfaced, according to the Missouri State Highway Patrol.

"He saw the love of his life in distress, and he was going to help his friend and do what a good human would do," Padgett said. "He gave his life helping someone else."

Padgett said Marsh was loving, hardworking and guided by his Christian faith, emphasizing that he never hesitated when someone needed help.

"There's nothing he wouldn't do for anyone," Padgett said. "You didn't have to tell him. You didn't have to beg him. He just was willing and would jump in there and do whatever it took to help someone."

Padgett said she had lost her only son in a fatal accident four years earlier. She began calling Marsh her son soon after he started dating her daughter.

"We instantly made a connection and a bond," she said. "I called him son, and he called me mama."

A motorcade escorted Marsh's body through Northwest Arkansas on Monday as people lined up along the route to honor him. Padgett said the response from law enforcement and the community showed the impact Marsh had made on many others.

"They made it very clear that Fred was not just their family, but so was my daughter, my family and, even more importantly, Fred's family," Padgett said.

Marsh was in his first year with the Rogers Police Department. He graduated from the Arkansas Law Enforcement Training Academy in April and only recently started working as an officer.

Nypd Officer Shot, Gunman Killed After Armed Barricaded Standoff In Brooklyn: Police

A GoFundMe created for Hailey by her sister to cover her lease, bills and other unforeseen expenses has raised nearly $2,000 as of Thursday morning.

"Fred was an upstanding young man- Son, Fiancée, Officer, Brother, Friend, and more to all. We are devastated and will miss him dearly," the fundraiser reads.

Funeral arrangements are being handled by Marsh's family, and Padgett said the family expects officers, former classmates, childhood friends and others from across the state to attend.

"Let's do something in Fred's honor," Padgett said. "Be kind to your fellow man. When Fred loved, he loved with everything he had, and he loved well."

title: Amish Shah wins Democratic congressional primary in Arizona, a blow to the party establishment
description: Amish Shah won the Democratic primary Wednesday in a hotly contested congressional district in Arizona, delivering another defeat to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which backed a riv...
fullText:
PHOENIX (AP) — Amish Shah won the Democratic primary Wednesday in a hotly contested congressional district in Arizona, delivering another defeat to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which backed a rival, as more voters reject the preferences of party leaders in Washington.

Shah, an emergency physician, will face Republican Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker who was endorsed by President Donald Trump in his primary, in the fall. Before becoming political opponents, Feely and Shah were part of the same team — the New York Jets. Shah was a doctor on the sidelines, while Feely was the kicker.

The DCCC backed Marlene Galán-Woods, a former Republican who switched parties at the beginning of Trump's first term.

The competition for the 1st Congressional District, an affluent area that includes northeast Phoenix, Scottsdale, Fountain Hills and Paradise Valley, is expected to help determine control of the U.S. House. Although Republicans hold a voter registration advantage, the district has shifted toward the center over the last decade.

The seat is open because Republican Rep. David Schweikert ran for governor, losing to Rep. Andy Biggs in the GOP primary on Tuesday.

The DCCC's decision to endorse Galán-Woods, a former television journalist in Phoenix, puzzled local Democrats because there was little ideological difference between her and Shah. Both are moderates, and the race was not a proxy fight in the party's deepening feud between progressives and centrists.

"Our victory in this primary was a grassroots victory where Arizona voters made their voices heard," Shah said Wednesday night in a statement that did not address the DCCC snub. "Now, it's my job to earn the support of every voter in this district."

Rep. Suzan DelBene, the DCCC Chair, issued a statement calling Feely an "extremist" and saying Shah "will always put his community first," but did not address the controversy surrounding the support for Galán-Woods.

The National Republican Congressional Committee quickly released a digital ad Wednesday attacking Shah, labeling him a socialist and tying him to progressives in Congress.

"I'm a political outsider committed to delivering results," Feely said in a statement.

The race was in some ways a replay of 2024, when Shah narrowly won in a crowded primary field that included Galán-Woods and lost in the general election. The DCCC did not endorse in the primary that year but backed Shah in the general.

The DCCC announced its support for Galán-Woods in May, when it added her to a list of candidates it was supporting in Republican-controlled districts. At the time, DelBene talked up Galán-Woods' experience in broadcast journalism but said nothing about Shah.

"I wasn't exactly my party's pick," Shah told supporters Tuesday night. "And I was willing to stand up to that establishment. And that's what the voters of this district want."

Still, he has said he would work with the DCCC if nominated. He will need support from the party and its donors to win what's likely to be a tough race in a district Trump carried narrowly in 2024. Former Democratic President Joe Biden won the district in 2020 even as Schweikert was reelected.

Antiestablishment fervor has spooked congressional leaders, who fear that swing voters will see some insurgent candidates as too extreme and squander Democrats' opportunity to take advantage of Trump's unpopularity.

Last month progressive Randy Villegas beat a DCCC-backed candidate for a top battleground district in California's Central Valley. And similarly in Maine, Matt Dunlap defeated a more moderate rival backed by the party.

DCCC support generally brings an influx of money and staffing, both from the party itself and from the donors and interest groups that take its cues. But establishment support has been a turnoff for some voters.

"The Democratic Party needs to grow up and wake up," said Maria Liong, a 24-year-old medical student who volunteered for Shah's campaign. "They need to realize that they want candidates who listen to their people."

In the GOP primary, Feely defeated Joseph Chaplik, a former state lawmaker popular with grassroots activists, for the party's nomination. He was in the NFL with seven teams over 14 seasons, including with the Arizona Cardinals from 2010 to 2013. He became an NFL broadcaster after retiring in 2014.

Feely and Shah overlapped on the Jets during the 2008 and 2009 seasons, when Shah worked home games as an airway management physician, according to his campaign. Every NFL game has an airway management doctor on the sideline to intubate and resuscitate a catastrophically injured player.

"It's an old relationship," Feely said of Shah on Tuesday night, before it was clear which Democrat he would face in November. "But whoever it is, I want to do this the right way. I want to run this the right way."

This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Rep. Suzan DelBene's last name on first reference, from DeBene.

title: Top House Democrat says anti-Israel activists’ threats kept him from town halls for a year
description: Rep. Adam Smith said he hasn't held a town hall in over a year after anti-Israel activists screamed death threats at him and threatened his wife.
fullText:
A senior House Democrat divulged this week that he has not been able to hold a town hall for over a year due to threats from anti-Israel activists.

Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the lead Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, made the explosive claim in an interview with "Breaking Points" on Tuesday.

"This is my biggest problem with the left," Smith said. "I have been unable to hold a town hall meeting for a year because a bunch of leftists show up and scream at me and don't let anyone else speak.

"You talk about illiberal," he continued. "Having people stand out in front of my house, screaming death threats at me and threatening my wife."

Jewish California Congressional Candidate Says Harassment From Gaza Agitators Went 'Beyond Free Speech'

Smith, a member of the Democratic Party's establishment wing, has previously condemned far-left activists who vandalized his home in 2023 over his support for Israel, including spray-painting "baby killer" in red on his garage doors.

"And the left [says], 'Oh, well, of course, we don't support [that]. We're peace activists. We would never do something like that.' OK. How about you just say, 'No, they did it. It's wrong. We're against it. We are going to be liberal.'"

He also recounted attending a hearing at the University of Washington during which pro-Israel speakers were shouted down by far-left activists during a debate on divesting from the Jewish state.

"So, the first three people got up and testified in favor of divesting. [The] fourth person got up and testified against divesting," Smith said in the "Breaking Points" interview. "Two sentences in, [they were] shouted down, screamed at, wouldn't stop.

"I think that whole thing has created a major problem as well," he added. "And we have to be able to have an intellectual discussion."

Fbi Nabs 7 For Alleged 'Campaign Of Violence' To Pressure University Of Michigan, Businesses Over Israel Ties

Smith also said the left has dubbed him a "Trump supporter" for pushing respectful debate.

He held up socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as an example of civility on the left.

"I don't agree with everything that he's doing, but he's having legitimate, thoughtful conversations instead of screaming matches over who can threaten the loudest," Smith reflected.

The Washington Democrat is not the only member of the House Democratic Caucus who has faced harassment from anti-Israel activists.

A New York City coffee chain told Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., in June that he was not welcome at its storefronts over his support for Israel.

Days later, Goldman, who is Jewish, lost re-election to Brad Lander, a Mamdani-backed challenger, who put criticism of the Jewish state at the center of his campaign.

Fox News Digital reached out to Smith for comment.
