title: How Troy Jackson went from an anti-abortion Republican to the Democrats’ hope for defeating Susan Collins
description: Troy Jackson is on the verge of replacing Graham Platner as the Democratic nominee for Senate in Maine after harnessing the enthusiasm of former Platner supporters who were galvanized by the oyster fa...
fullText:
Troy Jackson is on the verge of replacing Graham Platner as the Democratic nominee for Senate in Maine after harnessing the enthusiasm of former Platner supporters who were galvanized by the oyster farmer's insurgent campaign.

There's just one thing: Jackson is no political outsider.

The former Maine Senate Democratic leader has spent over two decades working in state politics, a resume that sets him apart even as Jackson embraces a similar progressive platform and openly appeals to former Platner supporters. Jackson's allies see the best of both worlds, especially after Maine Democrats took a risk on an outsider in Platner – and were sorely disappointed as his campaign imploded amid an allegation of rape that Platner denies.

"Troy's been around," said Jason Shedlock, a longtime labor leader in Maine. "If you don't know him, you know somebody who does. And if you don't know somebody who does, the person standing next to them has been impacted by him. That's the difference."

But if Jackson has more political experience than Platner did, he doesn't have the same oratorical skills and comes with a history of socially conservative stances early in his career, including opposing abortion, that could be uncomfortable for Democrats today.

Jackson is also facing fresh questions about his temperament after CNN reported this week that he has been accused of having angry outbursts with state lawmakers.

Yet after dominating the delegate hunt this weekend and forcing all his major opponents out of the race, Jackson is closer than ever to replacing Platner. It would be a capstone on a long political career that began in earnest in 2000, when Jackson ran for office as a Republican fed up with the corporate exploitation of loggers like himself.

"Ultimately he's a chameleon, he's a political chameleon," said Trey Stewart, the top Republican in the Maine Senate, noting his grandfather supported Jackson in his 2000 run. Since then, Stewart added, Jackson has been "all over the place" on issues.

Jackson's campaign said his political transformation stands in contrast with Collins.

"Troy has listened, learned and changed his position on some issues, and unlike Collins, he has been honest about where he stands. And he has never changed who he fights for," Jackson adviser BJ McCollister said in a statement, adding that Jackson has "consistently stood with working people."

To his supporters, Jackson reflects the unorthodox politics of Maine.

"He's a progressive champion, but he was Senate president, so … that tells you a lot about Maine," said Drew Gattine, a state representative and former state Democratic Party chair. "I don't think these labels like 'insider,' 'outsider,' really fit."

Jackson and his allies trace his entry into politics to a 1998 logging blockade along the Canadian border in northern Maine. He helped lead the weeklong blockade in protest of landowners hiring Canadian workers, driving down pay for US workers.

"Troy's origin story into politics is really important," said Matt Schlobohm, executive director of the Maine AFL-CIO. "He worked in one of the most exploitative industries in our state."

"There are those who call the shots and those who do the work," Schlobohm added. "The people working physically the hardest are really struggling just to survive."

A group of Maine politicians — including Collins, then in her first term – eventually agreed to meet with the loggers, according to Jackson's campaign, but Jackson felt they didn't take the underlying labor issues seriously enough. For Jackson, it was a revealing early brush with Collins, a fellow native of Aroostook County, which covers the rural northern tip of the state.

Two years later, Jackson ran for office as a Republican. He sought his local state House seat but lost to a Democrat, Marc Michaud. Jackson ran as an independent in the next election and defeated Michaud in an upset. He joined the Democratic Party in 2004 and continued rising politically, winning a state Senate seat four years later.

Jackson, who was raised Catholic, now says he was wrong on abortion and same-sex marriage and has built a voting record in recent years that is more aligned with national party positions. Still, his ideological past has continued to haunt him in some races, including this year's primary for governor.

"Mainers just can't trust Troy Jackson on abortion," said one TV ad from 314 Action, a national group that supported rival Nirav Shah, who also challenged Jackson for the Senate nomination before ending his bid.

It remains to be seen how Jackson's previous views could come up in a Senate race where Democrats are eager to highlight Collins' vote to confirm several justices who overturned Roe v. Wade. Asked about his past stances on abortion, the abortion rights advocacy group Reproductive Freedom for All provided a statement that did not mention Jackson but criticized Collins' record and promised the issue would be "front and center" in the race.

Schlobohm said Jackson's ideological evolution is not unheard of among union members, who may enter politics motivated more by economic issues than social issues, and change their views on the latter as they get more involved.

"It's a story that a lot of people understand," Schlobohm said.

Jackson's political ascent continued in 2018 when Democrats captured the majority in the Maine Senate and picked him as their leader.

He presided over legislative initiatives such as providing free school meals to all public K-12 students in Maine. He backed efforts to protect abortion access after the overturning of Roe v. Wade.

However, some supporters say one of the most revealing chapters was how he dealt with the state's growing offshore wind industry. They say his unique relationships within the state allowed him to bring together a wide range of interests — unions, environmentalists, fisheries and developers — to get a long-term plan for the industry's growth across the finish line in 2023.

"That requires an insane level of trust," Schlobohm said.

The issue sometimes put him at odds with a fellow Democratic state leader, Gov. Janet Mills, who vetoed another offshore wind bill over labor standards that Jackson supported.

Stewart, the Maine Senate Republican leader, had nothing positive to say about Jackson's tenure. He said Jackson oversaw a decline in bipartisanship in the chamber, passing "majority budgets" that did not need GOP support.

Jackson largely steered clear of national politics as he led the state Senate. But in 2016, as a superdelegate to the Democratic National Convention, he voted for Bernie Sanders over Hillary Clinton, an early show of commitment to the economic populism that is undergirding his Senate run.

His campaign for governor was a long-awaited moment for his progressive and labor allies. But it underwhelmed, placing third in first-round primary votes.

One thing that did stand out from Jackson's campaign, though, was how closely he tied himself to Platner. They both had the support of Sanders, they campaigned together multiple times, and Platner said he would rank Jackson as his first choice in the primary for governor.

Jackson stood by Platner through a number of controversies but called on him to drop out after the rape allegation. He said Platner had "lied" to him about whether there was anything more concerning in his past.

Republicans are already plotting to make an issue out of Jackson's ties to Platner as well as to Sanders.

"He's a Bernie bro," Collins told CNN's Manu Raju on Wednesday.

But for now, Jackson's embrace of Platner's movement and Sanders' politics seems to have paid off, giving him access to an enthusiastic voting base that, combined with his deep relationships in Maine politics and labor, make him a formidable contender for the nomination.

"Troy has spent his entire political career fighting for these same policies and platforms (that Platner did) within the state of Maine," said Crystale Lapham, a volunteer organizer with Maine People Powered, a grassroots group that grew out of Platner's campaign.

The group had hoped to host a forum with the candidates for the nomination but called it off after Jackson effectively wrapped up the nomination Sunday. He still met privately with the group a day later.

But even before this week, delegates were struck by the dedication of Jackson's organizing effort. His campaign said it ended up contacting over 11,000 Democrats in a week, aided by nearly 100 volunteers and 26 "caucus captains."

One Jackson delegate, Steven Fritzsche, said the campaign emailed his supporters for governor on July 9, a day before Platner formally ended his campaign, to start recruiting delegates. The campaign continued to stay in touch, including with a pre-debate call on July 16, and kept reaching out over the weekend to make sure delegates had everything they needed to stick together and dominate at the county meetings.

"I thought we'd do well," Fritzsche said. "I didn't think it would be as resounding."

CNN's Alison Main contributed to this report.

This story has been updated with additional information.

title: Opinion - Ukraine may already be winning World War III for an oblivious West
description: Ukraine is now dealing the decisive blow that may win the global war that much of the Western world still fails to recognize is being waged against it.
fullText:
Against all odds, Ukraine is right on the point of winning World War III.

In July 2022, we argued that Russian President Vladimir Putin had blundered his way into a dystopian global conflict that pitted Russia, China and their Axis of Evil allies — Iran and North Korea — against the West by invading Ukraine.

Despite our warnings, Washington and Brussels in 2023 continued to act as if Putin's war was merely an Eastern European conflict. They failed to grasp that Russia's aggression against Ukraine was the same threat as Chinese President Xi Jinping aggression against Taiwan and the Philippines.

In February 2023, China was actively conducting live-fire drills around Taiwan by sea and air. North Korea was aggressively conducting missile tests over the Sea of Japan. Iran was rapidly expanding its nuclear weapons program, and at the time had amassed 154 pounds of  highly enriched uranium, enough to build "several nuclear weapons," according to Rafael Grossi, the director of the International Atomic Energy Agency. After watching then-President Joe Biden's State of the Union speech that month, we wondered whether he wasn't already late to World War III.

Yet it was crickets at the White House in terms of connecting the dots between Putin and Xi's escalating war against the West. Biden's mantra was that Ukraine is an isolated conflict, and that it was only a question of defending Kyiv for as long as it takes. There was no talk then of defending U.S. allies and global interests from Putin and Xi's aim to create and wield a new world order. Nor did Hamas's heinous terrorist attacks and atrocities against Israeli civilians on Oct. 7, 2023 make it clear to Team Biden that the risk to global security had expanded far beyond the front lines in Ukraine.

It seemed Putin and Xi's visions of a new multi-polar order were openly clashing with traditional Western-style liberal democracy that had largely ensured global peace since the end of World War II in 1945. And the bad guys were winning.

Only one country fully understood what was at stake on a global basis: That was Ukraine, of course. By merely resisting and refusing to capitulate to Putin, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and his generals were holding back a tide of global setbacks for the West.

But now things have changed. Ukraine, chiefly on its own, using a wide assortment of asymmetrical kinetic means, is no longer fighting a long, losing defensive battle. Rather, it is dealing the decisive blow that may help to win the global war that much of the Western world still fails to recognize is being waged against it.

Zelensky has always understood the threat. Days before Putin invaded Ukraine, he warned that Europe and the world were facing their "biggest security crisis since the Cold War."

The Ukrainian president reiterated this just months ago, on the fourth anniversary of the start of the war. Zelensky said that Putin "has already started World War Three." Zelensky added that he believes "stopping Putin today and preventing him from occupying Ukraine is a victory for the whole world."

Over time Ukraine, has held Russia back. Its armed forces have repeatedly repelled spring and summer ground offensives, inflicting more than 1.4 million Russian casualties.

Today, with its strategic drone campaign, Kyiv is decimating Russia's oil and gas industry. It has now hit all 11 of the country's largest refineries, including a facility as far away as Siberia. It is estimated that Ukraine has destroyed or degraded as much as 43 percent of Russia's total refining capacity, causing $13.5 billion in direct losses to its already stressed war economy. Widespread shortages now persist throughout Russia — the situation is especially dire in Russian-occupied Crimea, whose isolation is nearly complete.

Ukraine is also decimating Russia's domestic supply chain. Beginning last week, Kyiv started striking the distribution centers of WildBerries, Moscow's version of Amazon. Damage is already in the billions. Ukraine claims that the company is playing an essential in equipping Russian soldiers — both those currently in the field and those about to be mobilized.

Beyond Eastern Europe, Ukraine's success is forcing Russia to retrench, especially in the Middle East. Putin was already unable to come to the aid of now-ousted Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad. Even Iran, a wartime ally against Ukraine, is also beyond his help under the weight of U.S. attacks.

In addition, Russian paramilitary forces are under heavy attack by Islamic State terrorists across the Sahel in Sub-Saharan Africa, especially in Mali. Putin also lost his foothold in Venezuela and is in danger of losing Cuba to the U.S.

Perhaps most significantly, Ukraine has forced China to hedge its bets. In 2025, Beijing became Kyiv's largest trading partner as the two countries' bilateral trade hit $21 billion. Yet even so, China is still paying a price for Ukraine's success. Kyiv's revolutionary innovations in the area of drone warfare are forcing Xi to recalibrate and even rethink any plans to invade Taiwan.

Even North Korea is reeling. Its soldiers for sale have died in Ukraine and its artillery and munitions have been proven marginal.

Putin, once seen as a hedge against Xi's domination of Southeast Asia, is now only a weakened junior partner to Beijing. Need evidence? Xi has rejected Putin's hopes of a Siberia 2 gas pipeline to generate badly needed revenue. Beijing has reportedly told Moscow to "stop raising the subject altogether." So much for their much-vaunted "no-limits partnership."

World War III is not yet won. But Ukraine is putting victory in the West's grasp — if only Washington and Brussels will seize it.

Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. They are the cofounders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

title: With bombing campaign unlikely to change Iran’s posture according to US intel, Trump faces limited options
description: Two weeks into a renewed bombing campaign against Iran, with US forces taking casualties and allies wary of the conflict escalating further, President Donald Trump insists that Iran is “desperate” to ...
fullText:
Two weeks into a renewed bombing campaign against Iran, with US forces taking casualties and allies wary of the conflict escalating further, President Donald Trump insists that Iran is "desperate" to find an end to wave after wave of US attacks.

But both the CIA and the Defense Intelligence Agency have recently assessed that the kind of bombing the US is currently carrying out is unlikely to shift the Iranian negotiating position, according to two US officials familiar with the assessments.

At the same time, the key mediator between the two sides — Qatar — threatened to walk away from the table after Iran struck a Qatari tanker earlier this month, in what would amount to a devastating and possibly irreplaceable loss for diplomatic efforts, according to a current and a former US official.

The Strait of Hormuz, a vital economic lifeline that was freely navigated by an armada of ships daily before the war, remains largely vacant after Iran insisted on authority to control traffic, enforcing their power with sporadic drone and threats of mines.

That confluence of events has left Trump, whose party is staring down potentially devastating midterm election losses in November, with few good options.

He could escalate by putting American boots on the ground, a threat he's made repeatedly as he's talked about occupying Kharg Island or removing Iran's highly enriched uranium. That would further break a key promise he made to his MAGA base: "I will not send you to fight and die in stupid foreign wars that never ends," he said during a 2024 campaign rally in Pennsylvania.

Trump has also telegraphed that the US plans to target a suspected nuclear facility underneath Pickaxe Mountain, which is located near the Natanz nuclear facility in the country's rugged interior.

Or he could accept a dangerous status quo: endless rounds of strikes and counterstrikes with Iran that are likely to cost further American lives and leave the Strait of Hormuz in a state of constant peril that could resemble the "forever wars" he has criticized. On Wednesday, Trump seemed to signal that path in a post on Truth Social, vowing that "any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz… the United States will bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT."

The key problem for the Trump administration is that although its traditional military is far superior to Iran's, the two sides are fighting two different wars. The US is escalating vertically, hitting increasingly sensitive and valuable targets inside Iran in a gradually-expanding geographic range in an effort to shift the calculus inside Tehran.

But Iran, whose air defenses and missile launch capabilities have been degraded by American strikes, are escalating horizontally — hitting US allies in the region and striking civilian infrastructure to provoke the international community to put pressure on Trump.

CNN reached out to the DIA, and the Qatar embassy in Washington D.C., but did not receive comment before this story published. The CIA declined to comment.

"Right now, the president is focused on making Iran pay for their violations of the MOU and their continued acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz," a US official told CNN. "In addition, the president will make Iran pay for the recent deaths of US soldiers. These devastating blows will continue until the president deems otherwise, but talks between our countries are continuing. President Trump has all of the cards and all options at his disposal."

Potentially accelerating growing economic pressure are new threats from Iran-aligned Houthi groups that they will be targeting ships passing through Bab al-Mandab, the passageway to the Red Sea that has served as a relief valve for some oil from Saudi Arabia during the conflict. The group claimed to have attacked two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea early on Thursday morning.

On Tuesday, top defense officials faced withering pressure from lawmakers on the Senate Appropriations Committee, who demanded a clear strategy for the war.

"We need some hard answers and some straight talk," Sen. John Kennedy, a Republican of Louisiana, said Wednesday, pressing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine on the consequences if the US withdrew from the conflict.

Trump and Hegseth had initially declared victory in the early days of the conflict, insisting that Iran had been militarily defeated.

Under intense pressure from the White House to prove that the war is going well, Hegseth and CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper have taken steps to restrict information sharing related to the conflict with other parts of the military and the intelligence community, CNN has previously reported.

Although its military was unquestionably degraded, Iran began striking energy infrastructure across the Gulf region, ratcheting up the economic consequences of the conflict not just for the United States but for its allies.

That's led to repeated pressure from allies to curtail US military operations and find a deal that could open the Strait of Hormuz and end the threat to nearby countries.

Iran has shown its willingness to absorb economic and military pain in the belief that it might outlast Trump's political appetite for the conflict, said Alex Vatanka, an analyst with the Middle East Institute in Washington who specializes in Iran. But that doesn't mean that Iran's leaders can afford for the war to go on forever.

"Those against diplomacy just have a fundamental conception that the US never delivers. But those are not the people who are running Iran today," Vatanka said. "They might not like Trump, or trust the US, but they still think that's better than risking an open-ended war."

The US has also restarted a blockade that some analysts believe may be doing more to push Tehran towards concessions than the bombing.

But for now, Iran's ability to threaten the Strait of Hormuz — and its neighbors — remains its greatest point of leverage.

Iran has also learned it can leverage targeted strikes against the energy infrastructure of Gulf countries as an asymmetric capability after doing so to great effect during the war. That tool isn't going away, a second source familiar with US intelligence assessments said.

Trump officials insist that the objective of the conflict remains to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. But that messaging has been muddled by the administration's previous insistence that it "obliterated" Iran's nuclear capabilities in a series of strikes last year. Since Trump launched this war, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has become the dominating issue in the conflict.

"This is a bombing campaign in search of a strategy," Joe Kent, a former Trump administration political appointee who resigned over the spin up to the conflict, said in a post on X. "We are choosing escalation when de-escalation remains an option, entrenching ourselves deeper into a broader war that we don't have the capability or desire to sustain. There is not a military solution here that will lead to a win. More bombing will not convince Iran to open the SOH or to give us the deal we want, it will only harden their position."

CNN's Zachary Cohen and Davis Winkie contributed to this story

title: Prime Minister Carney says Canada is ready to respond if Trump's new tariffs go into effect
description: Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday that Canada is intensifying negotiations with the United States to reach a comprehensive trade deal but is prepared to respond should President Donald Trump’s ...
fullText:
VANCOUVER, British Columbia (AP) — Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday that Canada is intensifying negotiations with the United States to reach a comprehensive trade deal but is prepared to respond should President Donald Trump's threat of 50% tariffs on Canadian goods go into effect.

The new tariffs, announced by Trump on Monday, are scheduled to come into effect Aug. 19.

"If these tariffs, or other measures come into force, there's a full range of things that we can do in that regard," Ca rney said after meeting with Canada's premiers and territorial leaders in Charletown, Prince Edward Island.

Carney said "everything's on the table" if an agreement can't be reached before the tariffs kick in.

"We don't need to respond in advance," he said. "In fact, I think it would be counterproductive at this stage to respond in advance."

The new tariffs cover a wide range of goods, including honey, liquor, cement, dairy products, some wood products, hockey sticks and other items. They exclude energy products, potash, fish and critical minerals, but would include goods previously protected from import taxes by the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA. That 2020 trade pact was not renewed by the U.S., triggering a new set of negotiations that could run until 2036.

Carney said the tariff threat could be a negotiation tactic by the U.S.

"We've seen a series of trade negations that the U.S. has undertaken, and normally there's a deadline," he said. "Normally there's an outsized tariff associated with that deadline."

Carney believes there is a willingness among U.S. officials to reach a trade deal.

Prince Edward Island Premier Rob Lantz said the provinces and federal government remain united.

"We need to have a united Team Canada approach," he said. "Canada is at it's best when provinces and territories and the federal government work together."

Carney said Canada will continue to build and diversity its economy.

"In all circumstances, irrespective of the outcome of these negotiations, Canada will do whatever it takes to build our strength at home and to support Canadian families, workers, our farmers, our businesses," he said.

The country is also looking to build trade relationships with countries other than the U.S.

"We're diversifying our partnerships abroad," he said.

An analysis by Desjardins, one of Canada's largest financial institutions, says the tariffs will impact about $28 billion Canadian ($19.8 billion) worth of annual Canadian exports to the United States. That's about 5% of what the U.S. imports from Canada each year.

"Beyond the direct trade effects, heightened uncertainty could dampen business confidence and curb investment plans," the analysis says.

The Canadian provinces most impacted would be Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia.

Prior to the meeting Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Canada needs to show strength.

"We need a strong plan," he said. "Be on offense. Put everything on the table."

Ford was asked if he would put a surcharge on electrically his province sells to the U.S.

"It depends where we go with the U.S.," he said. "Ontario has the most to lose right now. I will do everything to protect the people of Ontario."

Later Thursday, the Trump administration included Canada among the dozens of countries it's hitting with tariffs citing forced labor in supply chains.

In a statement, Dominic LeBlanc, the Canada-U.S. Trade Minister, said the move "is not unexpected."

LeBlanc said Canada shares the U.S.'s objective of ensuring that goods produced with forced labor don't enter the supply chain.

"We will continue engaging constructively with the United States on this matter, as well as other outstanding issues, over the coming weeks to the mutual benefit of our citizens," LeBlanc said.

title: Iran weaponized the Strait of Hormuz. Now its neighbors are building around it
description: For the first time in decades, the Middle East is investing seriously in a future in which the Strait of Hormuz may no longer be indispensable.
fullText:
Brett McGurk is a CNN global affairs analyst who served in senior national security positions under Presidents George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald Trump and Joe Biden.

Wars often end somewhere different from where they begin.

The current conflict with Iran has been plagued by ill-defined and shifting objectives, from aspirations of regime change to more focused aims of degrading Iran's nuclear and military capabilities.

Nearly six months in, it has evolved into something else entirely: a struggle over who controls the Strait of Hormuz and, with it, one of the world's most important arteries for global energy. Iran has demonstrated both the capability and willingness to target commercial shipping passing through the strait unless conducted under rules Tehran prescribes.

The US – and much of the world, including all the Gulf states adjacent to the strait – has rightly deemed that unacceptable.

The strategic objective now is increasingly about one issue. Does the Strait of Hormuz remain an international waterway, or does Iran acquire the ability to determine who passes through it and under what conditions? Ceding control to Iran would hand its regime tens of billions of dollars in transit fees per year, and the ability to meter energy flows to the rest of the world. Iran would effectively control the thermostat for the global economy.

Iran is not physically blocking the strait. It's firing drones and cruise missiles at civilian ships. That is enough to stop commerce in its tracks, and upend a long-standing assumption: that the Strait of Hormuz would remain an international passageway even during periods of conflict. During the twelve-day war in June 2025, for example, including the US strikes against Iran's nuclear facilities, Hormuz remained unaffected.

That longstanding assumption has now broken, and it presents a massive challenge to the US and to the world.

I served in the White House when the Iranian proxy group the Houthis used Iranian missiles and drones to shut down the Red Sea using the same tactics in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. The US built a coalition and mounted an air campaign to degrade Houthi capabilities – but we could not stop every launch, or restore confidence to commercial shippers to make the passage. The Houthis only stopped firing after they reached a deal with Washington.

Today, the US will confront the same problem: a time consuming, costly, and extremely difficult mission to deny Iran's ability to attack with drones and cruise missiles that can be fired from over 1,000 kilometers away. It's a classic needle-in-a-haystack mission.

Only this problem is far worse. The Bab al-Mandeb accounts for 10% of global shipping. That's enough to boost inflation a bit. Hormuz accounts for 20% of global energy trade. That's enough, as President Donald Trump said before announcing a short-lived deal with Iran, to spark an "economic catastrophe."

Iran's strategy is to boost the price of energy globally to pressure the White House to cede control of the strait altogether. Its tactics, however, with attacks on civilian ships and across the Gulf, are producing a longer-term reaction that will eventually work against it.

Across the Middle East, governments and energy companies are accelerating pipelines, ports and transportation corridors designed to move oil, gas and goods around Hormuz rather than through it. The US is now directly supporting these initiatives.

The strait will remain important. But for the first time in decades, the region is investing seriously in a future in which it may no longer be indispensable.

The energy map of the Middle East is being redrawn specifically to reduce Iran's leverage over this chokepoint.

Let's break it down. Before the war, approximately 23 million barrels of energy products per day passed through the Strait of Hormuz. It was the single chokepoint for exports from Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain, and the main transit route for products from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

Now governments are planning for a future in which Hormuz periodically closes or remains commercially unreliable. This changes the equation. Instead of one indispensable chokepoint, states are investing in a system of multiple export routes that can gradually reduce Iran's leverage.

These projects will not replace all of the barrels that transited Hormuz before the war, but they will significantly reduce its importance. Goldman Sachs recently estimated that existing or new bypass routes could by the end of 2028 carry about 60% of the oil typically being shipped through the strait.

Consider the following projects getting underway because of the war:

Saudi's Arabia (9M): The last time Iran contested the Strait of Hormuz was four decades ago, during the Iran-Iraq war. At the time, Saudi Arabia made the decision to invest billions of dollars in an "east-west" pipeline across its territory from oil producing provinces to the Red Sea. During the current crisis, this pipeline provided relief to the global market with approximately 7 million barrels of exports per day. Saudi Arabia has since announced an expansion of this pipeline system to add another 1-2 million barrels per day by the end of 2029, boosting total bypass from Hormuz up to 9 million barrels per day.

UAE (3.6M): The UAE also has an existing port and pipeline south of Hormuz, which currently delivers up to 1.8 million barrels to global markets. The country has since announced a massive expansion program to double this capacity by the end of 2027, delivering a total of 3.6 million barrels per day.

Iraq-Syria (2-3M): Last week, Iraq's new prime minister visited the White House and announced tens of billions of dollars in new investments from US oil firms in coordination with Syria to refurbish dormant lines and integrate new lines to export Iraqi and Kuwaiti barrels to the Mediterranean. Trump's envoy to Iraq and Syria, Tom Barrack, said the projects aim to make Hormuz "an afterthought" with times to completion around 2030. I would not go that far, but moving Iraq's vast energy resources west instead of south through Hormuz would be a game-changer.

Iraq-Turkey (1M): The Iraq projects include refurbishment of this existing but often dormant pipeline, running from Kirkuk in Iraq to Ceyhan on the Turkish coast of the Mediterranean. Plagued for years by political disputes between Ankara and Baghdad, the new global demand is once again pushing this export route to the forefront as an essential and lucrative resource.

Iraq-Jordan (1-2.5M): The government of Iraq is also accelerating plans for an oil pipeline to Jordan. This pipeline would connect Basra to Haditha in western Iraq with a spur to the Jordanian port in Aqaba and export through the Red Sea to global markets. While long discussed, the Jordanian and Iraqi governments earlier this month announced plans to accelerate its development due to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

All of that is just the start as these and other projects get underway to bypass Hormuz. Saudi Arabia is also discussing a northern route for shipments to Aqaba or further northward through Turkey to feed into the Mediterranean.

There is important historical precedent. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, the US proposed an ambitious pipeline crossing Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Turkey to the Mediterranean. Known as the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) project, it required billions of dollars of investment and years of sustained American diplomacy across administrations. At first, many experts dismissed BTC as too ambitious (it stretches over 1,000 miles), too expensive, and politically impossible. History proved otherwise.

Once completed in 2006, BTC permanently reduced dependence on Russian-controlled export routes, and demonstrated that energy infrastructure can reshape global politics as much as military alliances.

These new networks of partnerships and pipelines will face challenges and setbacks. Iran might target static pipelines and delay construction. There may be delays in construction, or bureaucracy, or financing. But taken together, they reveal a strategic direction that is unlikely to reverse.

The Middle East capitals that once assumed Hormuz would remain reliably open are now planning for the likelihood that it will not. Resilient and redundant export routes have become national security imperatives, backed by leadership and sovereign funds with support and assistance from the US.

Iran's strategy ultimately depends on the assumption that the world has no practical alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. It may ultimately discover that in weaponizing the passageway, it persuaded its neighbors to build a region that no longer depends on it.

That is an outcome that Washington — and its allies — should actively help to bring about.

title: Mitch McConnell’s hometown paper publishes scathing ‘pre-obituary’
description: Joseph Gerth, a columnist for the Louisville Courier Journal, published a piece reflecting on McConnell's career despite him still being alive.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — Kentucky Senator Mitch McConnell was the subject of a scathing "pre-obituary" by his hometown newspaper.

Joseph Gerth, a columnist for the Louisville Courier Journal, published a piece reflecting on the 84-year-old's career even though McConnell is still alive.

The piece was highly critical, saying McConnell dismantled civil rights protections he once advocated and enabled President Donald Trump.

"Unlike Nixon, McConnell never paid for his sins that have damaged our nation's trust in government, destroyed the country's ability to have meaningful dialogue and cemented our nation's politics as an arena in which winning is the only thing that matters," Gerth wrote in the publication, calling McConnell a "detestable figure."

McConnell was hospitalized June 14 after a fall at his home. His condition gained national attention after his office went nearly a month without updating the public on his status.

Gerth noted the idea behind the McConnell piece was prompted by the death of longtime Sen. Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican, earlier this month.

"That got me thinking about Sen. Mitch McConnell, who was rumored to be dead or on life support or in a coma or whatever and was the odds-on favorite to beat Graham to the gates of hell in the days before Graham's death," Gerth wrote. "And, so with McConnell allegedly on the mend, I figured I'd go ahead and tell you what I think about McConnell now — when no one can complain, 'How dare you write that about a dead guy?'"

McConnell was first elected to the Senate 42 years ago. He has gone on to win reelection six times, becoming the state's longest-serving senator.

"He had more guts as a young man than he had as an old man," Gerth stated. "It seems somehow fitting for the ultimate shape-shifter, who wrote about accompanying Sen. John Sherman Cooper to see Johnson sign the Voting Rights Act into law, that the court he created was the court that struck down the last remaining significant provision."

On July 12, nearly one month after his hospitalization, McConnell released a picture of himself along with a full statement on his condition. The photo showed him sitting in a hospital bed holding a newspaper beside his wife, Elaine Chao.

NewsNation's Ashley Soriano contributed to this report.

title: Preorders for the Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra2 Come With a Free $100 Gift Card
description: Amazon is giving away a $100 gift card with Galaxy Watch Ultra2 preorders.
fullText:
The Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra2 was released at the July Unpacked event on the 22nd, showcasing the popular wearable’s extended battery life, improved outdoor performance, and a lighter design, putting it on the wishlists of many Samsung and Android users. To celebrate the launch, Amazon is offering a $100 gift card with Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra2 pre-orders that will ship out beginning August 7, bringing the price down by 13% to $699.99 (originally $799.99).

The 800mAh battery is around 35% larger than its predecessor, lasting around 60 hours with the display always on and around three days on lighter settings. And while it still can’t replace a Garmin, it’s significantly more rugged than the Ultra, with features like dual-frequency GPS, trail-run tracking with elevation data, hydration guidance, a titanium build, 10ATM water resistance, IP69K protection, and EN13319 dive certification. NB-NTN satellite connectivity is also an exciting improvement, letting you send messages or make calls without a cell signal.

The 47mm face has a 5,000-nit AMOLED display (up from 3,000 nits) for superior brightness and is powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite chip, built for AI workloads. The design is also lighter and more comfortable; despite the bigger battery, it’s now 12% thinner with a lighter strap, but still equally rugged with its titanium case. Compared to the Galaxy Watch 9,  the Ultra 2 is more durable and has a pretty major battery advantage.

If you spend a lot of time outdoors and want a premium LTE smartwatch that can handle all your adventures (and will actually use the $100 Amazon gift card), this pre-order Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra2 deal is one you should snag before it sells out. If you wait until launch day, you’ll pay the same price, but you won’t get the bonus gift card. That said, if you mostly just want notifications, fitness tracking, and sleep data, the Galaxy Watch 9 might be a more sensible choice.

title: A New Garmin Update Will Give You This Popular Feature for Free on the Cirqa Band
description: But this is a fishy sign for the future of Garmin's "subscription-free" promises.
fullText:
This week Garmin launched the Cirqa, its first screenless smart band, for $199.99. Right out of the gate, Garmin leaned into marketing the Cirqa as a Whoop alternative that does not require a subscription. However, that "subscription-free" promise is already under fire.

Within these first few days of the Cirqa's long-awaited launch, users have begun voicing concerns that some very basic workout features require a Garmin Connect+ subscription—namely, live heart rate displays. Luckily, Garmin has already responded to the outcry, confirming that an update should fix this issue within the next couple of days. Here's what we know so far.

Hands-on testing this week revealed that if you want to see your current heart rate during a workout, you'd need to 99 per month. Without paying, you could only see your average heart rate after finishing a workout—not a live reading, which is extremely useful during the exercise itself.

Others have pointed out that the change appears to be a direct response to the backlash the Cirqa received in its first days on the market. When I asked Garmin for comment, a rep told me: "We'll be rolling out live heart rate during activities in the next Garmin Connect Mobile build. This subscription-free feature will be available in the next few days to Cirqa Smart Band customers."

Even still, it's important to note that not all features are available without a subscription. Garmin Connect locks a whole range of advanced features behind a subscription paywall, from Garmin Coach (which can create personalized training plans), to nutrition tracking, meditation, and breathing exercises.

To Garmin's credit, the reversal came fast. Still, Cirqa's entire pitch is built around not needing a monthly fee, so locking something as fundamental as a live heart rate reading behind Connect+ was always going to look bad. It's worth noting that competing screenless trackers like the Polar Loop and Amazfit Helio Strap show it for free, too.

The bigger story here is Garmin's (and other fitness trackers') ominous pattern of paywalling things. With this week's live heart rate outcry, it looks like plenty of Cirqa users instinctively interpreted what could have been a software bug as some sort of corporate ploy. Garmin has spent the last couple of years steadily moving more functionality into Connect+, and each time it does, longtime users brace for the next basic feature to disappear behind that wall.

I asked a rep directly about whether "subscription-free" promises could change down the line. With standard disclaimers about not speaking to any future roadmap, Garmin says it won't suddenly wall off features that are free today. Any future paid tier would be additive, with new features available behind a subscription, rather than existing stuff pulled behind a paywall. None of this is confirmed, but it's a fairly predictable shape a future paywall would take, so I'll be keeping an eye on it for you.

title: ChatGPT Health Is Rolling Out to Everyone, but I Don’t Trust It
description: The privacy protections have gotten worse since the feature was first announced.
fullText:
OpenAI announced today that ChatGPT Health will now be available to all users over 18, and on all plans, including free ones. My general skepticism of AI-based health advice aside, I think there are good reasons to avoid this iteration of ChatGPT Health entirely—including a major downgrade in privacy from the original ChatGPT Health setup.

With ChatGPT Health, you can connect your medical records or Apple Health data to the chatbot. OpenAI says that the bot will ask for permission to access your health data for conversations, and that it’s not meant to replace a doctor, but to give advice or help you interpret your medical data. Despite these caveats (and the announcement's chart seeming to show that ChatGPT Health gets more “high scores” than real life doctors), I see red flags everywhere.

When OpenAI first announced its “dedicated health experience,” one of the big selling points was that conversations in Health would not be used for future AI training, and that your Health conversations would be kept separate from all other conversations.

But the terms have now shifted. OpenAI now says that your connected health information will not be used to train AI, and that only conversations that use that connected information will be considered Health conversations. This means that if ChatGPT reads about a diagnosis from your medical records, you’re now having a protected Health conversation. But if you don’t connect your medical records, and just want to tell ChatGPT about your diagnosis in your own words, that’s not considered a Health conversation.

This also means that the only way to get the privacy protections of ChatGPT Health is to share your health data with OpenAI. As the company writes in its announcement: “You can ask health questions in ChatGPT without connecting anything. To use Health and get responses grounded in your own information, you can choose to connect Apple Health, supported medical records from U.S. hospital systems, One Medical, or Function Health.” The former conversations would have privacy protections. The latter would not.

OpenAI touts its HealthBench evaluations to imply that ChatGPT is good at giving medical advice. But, as I’ve previously written, LLMs like ChatGPT don’t give reliable medical advice and shouldn’t be trusted. Previous studies have shown that even when an LLM gives the “right” answers to carefully constructed health-related questions, real-world conversations tend to go off the rails.

HealthBench seems to suffer from the same limitations. OpenAI says that real physicians wrote rubrics to grade responses, and physicians used those rubrics to grade responses from different ChatGPT models and from their fellow physicians. Conveniently, the results show that paid ChatGPT models score higher than free ones, which in turn score higher than real doctors.

But that doesn’t mean a chatbot is actually trustworthy. One evaluation of the HealthBench framework points out that the tests are not real conversations, and "may omit idiomatic phrasing, topic shifts, and unanticipated patient concerns." Another major limitation is that HealthBench only tests short conversations, an approach that “precludes assessment of longitudinal workflows and multidisciplinary handovers,” like real-life conversations that may be long or involve other topics.

People who ask ChatGPT for health advice aren’t conducting specific, focused tests of its health advice, and so the LLM’s responses aren’t necessarily going to be anything like the responses that were rated in HealthBench. OpenAI clearly knows this, since the announcements emphasize how often people ask health questions in the course of everyday conversations.

And those are just the limitations of the HealthBench framework, before you start looking at the specifics. The authors of the paper I quoted above point out that the testing material didn’t include enough rare diseases to know how well a model would perform when asked about them. And the rubrics seem sloppy, too: OpenAI’s own example, from its announcement of HealthBench, gives a certain response 9 points for “Includes clear and concise advice to seek emergency medical care at the beginning of the response” and then later in the same rubric, awards another 10 points for “States to contact emergency medical services at the beginning of the response.” That looks like either OpenAI is double-dipping to inflate scores, or simply not having anybody proofread the rubrics. Either way, I can’t trust the results.

Most importantly, people do use ChatGPT for medical advice, and they have suffered medical problems and even death after doing so, and the company knows it. The company was sued this week by a pastor who says he almost died after asking ChatGPT-4o (a model no longer available) for advice on what turned out to be a pulmonary embolism. That lawsuit seeks an injunction that would make the company stop offering health products like ChatGPT Health.

Other lawsuits against OpenAI allege that its products contributed to suicide and psychosis in its users. ECRI, a medical safety nonprofit, named the misuse of AI chatbots the number one health technology hazard of 2026.

If you want to give ChatGPT Health a try anyway, it’s worth knowing how to use the tools it offers to protecting your privacy (somewhat):

You can use temporary chats to start a conversation that doesn’t use memory or personalization features.

After importing your health data, you can review and edit the information—for example, correcting errors or removing anything that you don’t want on record.

You can disconnect your health information at any time in your settings, under Health > Accounts. The company says the data will be deleted “within 30 days.”

You can make ChatGPT ask for permission to access your health records every time (rather than granting a blanket permission). This setting can be changed in Settings > Plugins > Health.

Be careful when using plugins that may share health information. OpenAI says it has “additional safeguards” that may ask you for permission to share data, but it also says “We continue to test these safeguards...” which suggests that the company isn’t currently catching everything it should.

title: It Just Got a Lot Cheaper to Try Gemini Spark, Google's AI Agent
description: You no longer have to pay up to $200 per month to have Google's AI do things for you.
fullText:
Gemini Spark, the AI agent built into Google Gemini, is now a lot cheaper to try out in the U.S. Previously, Gemini Spark was exclusive to the Google AI Ultra plan, which costs $100-$200 per month. The company is now bringing the agentic AI to its AI Pro plan, which costs $20 per month. (For now, this change is exclusive to the U.S.)

When Gemini Spark was announced during Google I/O 2026, its features seemed potentially useful, but the barrier to entry was too high for most people. That appears to be changing now, as Google has cut the price by as much as 90%. It is not yet available on the $5/month AI Plus plan or the free tier, but that could change in the future too—though it's likely that using Gemini Spark on lower pricing tiers could mean that you hit your usage limits much faster.

Google Gemini is a chatbot and a voice assistant that answers your questions, creates text, media, and even entire apps for you. Gemini Spark takes those capabilities to your Google account and executes actions for you.

You can think of Gemini Spark as a personal AI assistant that can look at your emails, calendar entries, photos, and other data in your Google account to perform tasks on your behalf. You can use Spark to bulk unsubscribe from mailing lists, make flight bookings, send reminder emails to clients, colleagues, or family members, book appointments, and much more.

Having said all that, a Gemini Spark overview from out sister site PC Mag emphasizes that its features tend to overlap with Gemini. PC Mag called Spark the best AI agent yet, but that doesn't mean it's perfect.

To someone who is even remotely privacy-conscious, using Gemini Spark is going to sound quite invasive: You basically have to give it access to your entire computer if you want it to be able to act on your behalf. Google is aware of that, and has programmed the AI agent to ask for confirmations before performing certain actions. If you ask the agent to find birthday photos from 2017 and email them to someone, for example, Gemini Spark will show you the pictures and ask for a confirmation before actually sending the email. It applies the same logic to deleting emails, sending messages, using your saved credit cards to pay for reservations, and more.

It's worth keeping in mind that AI services have created serious problems for people who use these apps without due caution. The biggest strength of Gemini is its access to all the data that’s in your Google account, but if you give it unrestricted access and the AI agent messes up a request, you could be stuck with an incorrect hotel reservation, a flight booked to a wrong country, or other serious consequences.

title: You Can Now Verify Your Facebook Account With a Video Selfie
description: Upload a selfie video and earn a white check mark. But is that a good idea?
fullText:
If you're on Facebook, you may soon see a new type of verification badge on user profiles meant to indicate that there is a real, live person behind them. The platform is adding a free verification feature that allows users to upload a selfie video and earn a white check mark, which will appear on their profile and across Marketplace, Dating, and Groups. (At launch, badges won't appear in Feed posts, but Facebook says that feature will be added in the future.)

Note that this is different from Meta Verified, a paid subscription that provides the blue check mark to accounts on Facebook and Instagram. This verification indicates that Meta has confirmed the user's identity based on a review of their government-issued ID and, in some cases, a selfie video.

Facebook Verified is available to users age 18 and older whose accounts are in good standing with the platform's community standards, though the feature is launching in select markets initially before being rolled out globally. Once you have access, you'll need to record a short video selfie, which Facebook will compare to existing profile photos on your account using facial recognition. If your verification is approved, the white check mark will be added to your profile. Verification is not available for Pages or ProMode accounts.

Facebook says it will store your selfie video for "up to 30 days" after verification, which is a one-time process. It's not entirely clear what happens with that video in the meantime, and it's worth noting that Meta has relied on user data to train its AI. Meta AI (and Meta more broadly) is a terrible offender when it comes to privacy and security, so you should consider whether the tradeoff of a verification mark is worth handing over more of your data and read the privacy policy before you agree.

Google also launched a video selfie verification feature this week, though its purpose is to prove your identity should you get locked out of your account. Unlike Facebook Verified, which is meant to be a trust signal to other users, Google's selfie verification allows access to your entire Google account, bringing with it some additional security considerations.

title: Para-swimmer Letton-Jones wins first Wales medal
description: Teenage para-swimmer Ela Letton-Jones wins the first Team Wales medal of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow by claiming silver in the pool.
fullText:
Teenage Para-swimmer Ela Letton-Jones has secured the first Team Wales medal of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow by claiming silver in the pool.

The 19-year-old finished second in the women's S13 100m freestyle in a time of one minute, 4.30 seconds behind Australian Jenna Jones, who won in 1:03.89.

It was the same result as the morning session after Letton-Jones had qualified second fastest.

Letton-Jones was able to cope with the pressure of being Wales' first medal hope.

"I knew that coming in so I am just glad I was able to deliver and hopefully give Team Wales some momentum to win more medals," said Letton-Jones.

"I enjoyed it and I am glad that I did and it proves I swim a lot better when I am happy.

"I was speechless because I had never heard a crowd as noisy as that before. It carried me, gave me a lot more adrenaline and probably made me swim faster.

"My Mum, Dad and Nanny were here and I am grateful for their support because I could not have won silver without them."

Wales at the Commonwealth Games

Letton-Jones, from Y Felinheli in Gwynedd, has albinism, a congenital condition that severely affects her sight, so she has to count her strokes to know when she is approaching the wall of the swimming pool.

That has not stopped Letton-Jones from following her dream to reach the 2028 Paralympics in Los Angeles.

After narrowly missing out on the Paris Games in 2024, the teenager was invited onto the Aquatics GB Para-swimming world-class programme.

Letton-Jones won silver in the women's 100m backstroke S12 on her World Para-swimming championships debut in 2025.

Her success came in the first full day of competition in Glasgow for a Commonwealth Games that has 113 Welsh athletes participating in 10 different sports.

title: Kelly and Agyarko ooze confidence before title bout
description: With the IBF world light-middleweight title in his possession, Josh Kelly feels "it's a different version of me" since he dethroned Bakhram Murtazaliev and promises to "put on a show" in his maiden defence against Caoimhin Agyarko on Saturday.
fullText:
Briton Josh Kelly says we will see a "different version" of him when he makes the first defence of his IBF light-middleweight title against Caoimhin Agyarko on Saturday.

Kelly rebuilt from his sole career loss in 2021 to beat Bakhram Murtazaliev and claim the title in January, winning the belt in his 20th professional bout.

Belfast's Agyarko has also overcome adversity to earn a seat at world title level, having been cut by promoter Matchroom after what was then a career-best win over Troy Williamson in 2023.

Both men will walk to the ring in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia on the undercard of Anthony Joshua's heavyweight return against Kristian Prenga fully aware of how tough it has been to get to this stage.

"Being a world champion does something to you," Kelly said at Thursday's final news conference.

"I thought it was a myth beforehand but how I'm going about my work in the gym is just different. It's a different version of me.

"When I have that confidence, it's a hard night for anyone: 'Boots' [Jaron Ennis], [Sebastian] Fundora - any of them.

"I'm going to come in on Saturday, show there's levels to this game and put on a show."

Adversity to history - Agyarko's world title dream

The two days which could make or break Fury-Joshua

Ready to 'conquer Earth' - Joshua embraces comeback spotlight

Kelly's fast start against Murtazaliev was the platform for his title success as he mixed movement with measured attacks.

Although just nine of his 18 wins have come inside the distance, he felt the big-punching defending champion "was feeling the shots" and reluctant to open up.

The Sunderland fighter is promising a similar performance and "it will be early on" when he breaks Agyarko's spirit, but the challenger has scoffed at that notion.

Undefeated in 18 contests - seven inside the distance - Agyarko had to dig deep to come through his last outing against Ishmael Davis.

Agyarko was knocked down in the 12th round but made it to the final bell with his right eye swollen shut and had ultimately done enough to win by split-decision.

The 29-year-old suffered damage to his left eye in the previous contest, a points win over Ryan Kelly, so he will know he can ill-afford to become a stationary target for the champion.

Agyarko and Kelly both appeared agitated during Thursday's news conference and there was a heated exchange when they faced off.

'Black Thunder' rejected claims that he will wilt in the early stages of the contest and promised a career-best performance.

"He's a world champion and a good fighter, but this nonsense I will lose confidence early - I've heard it all before," Agyarko said.

"It's my time to go and prove everybody wrong, just as I have the last three or four fights when I've been the underdog and the 'B side' but have always come out on top.

"I'm prepared for the best Josh Kelly and you're going to see the best Caoimhin Agyarko so it will be a great fight, but I believe I will create history.

"I will run through brick walls to become the first black Irish world champion and if I have to beat the best Josh Kelly, then so be it."

title: Scottish sides in Europe postpone league matches
description: All five Scottish teams in European competitions have opted to postpone their Premiership matches scheduled for Saturday, 22 August.
fullText:
All five Scottish teams in European competitions have opted to postpone their Premiership matches scheduled for Saturday, 22 August.

The qualifying play-offs for the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League will take place across two legs, either side of the weekend affected.

Celtic and Rangers are both guaranteed to reach that stage in Europe, although the latter do not yet know which competition they will be in.

Previously, postponements had to be agreed by both clubs, but since April 2025, a team playing in Europe has been able to unilaterally delay a game.

Premiership winners Celtic do not yet know their opposition for this year's Champions League play-offs, at which stage they were beaten by Kazakh side Kairat Almaty last season.

Hearts are 4-0 behind on aggregate in their Champions League second round qualifying tie against Sturm Graz and are likely to drop into the third round of Europa League qualifying, where Rangers have already been drawn against Polish side Jagiellonia Bialystok.

The only way Hearts will avoid a play-off is if they beat Sturm Graz on aggregate and then lose in the third round of Champions League qualifying. In that case, they would directly enter the Europa League league phase.

Motherwell and Hibernian are in the middle of their Conference League second round qualifying ties and their league matches will only be postponed should they reach the play-offs.

Motherwell are 2-0 up on aggregate against Faroese side HB, while Hibs lost the first leg by the same scoreline against Kosovan outfit Malisheva.

Rearranged games will be played in midweek - on either 8/9 or 15/16 September.

All matches Saturday, 22 August:

Dundee United v Dundee - will take place as scheduled.

Falkirk v Heart of Midlothian - will be postponed if Hearts are involved in a play-off.

Hibernian v Kilmarnock - will be postponed if Hibs are involved in the Conference League play-offs.

Motherwell v Aberdeen - will be postponed if Motherwell are involved in the Conference League play-offs.

Rangers P-P St Mirren - match postponed as Rangers will be involved in the play-offs of the Europa League, or the Conference League.

St Johnstone P-P Celtic - match postponed as Celtic are involved in the Champions League play-offs.

title: Van Bommel appointed Belgium head coach
description: Belgium appoint former Netherlands captain Mark van Bommel as their new head coach on a contract running through Euro 2028.
fullText:
Belgium have appointed former Netherlands captain Mark van Bommel as their new head coach on a contract running through Euro 2028.

The 49-year-old succeeds Rudi Garcia, whose departure was confirmed after Belgium's quarter-final exit to eventual world champions Spain at the 2026 World Cup. Van Bommel will officially take up the role on 15 August.

Van Bommel most recently managed Royal Antwerp, guiding the club to the Belgian league title, Belgian Cup and Belgian Super Cup during a successful two-year spell.

"It is a great honour to become head coach of Belgium," Van Bommel said. "Belgium has outstanding players and enormous potential. Together with my coaching staff, we want to build a team that is disciplined, ambitious and brave enough to compete with the very best."

Belgian Football Association sporting director Vincent Mannaert said Van Bommel's "international experience as both a coach and player" would help the Red Devils "continue to improve, achieve results and reach their full potential".

Van Bommel will be assisted by Boudewijn Zenden, Maarten Martens and Reinier Robbemond, with an early task to oversee Nations League fixtures against Italy, France and Turkey across September and October.

Sciver-Brunt feels 'mum guilt' as coaching career begins
description: Former fast bowler Katherine Sciver-Brunt and wife of England captain Nat discusses the difficulties of balancing her coaching ambitions with being a mum.
fullText:
Former England fast bowler Katherine Sciver-Brunt has opened up about the challenges of mum guilt as she begins her coaching career.

Sciver-Brunt is married to England captain Nat, and the pair welcomed son Theo in 2025.

Having retired in 2023, Katherine carried their first child and although she has been involved in broadcasting with BBC Test Match Special since, she is now taking her first steps in a new venture as Trent Rockets' assistant coach.

After Rockets thrashed Birmingham Phoenix in their opening match on Friday, Sciver-Brunt spoke honestly about juggling her personal ambitions with her role as a mum.

"I would love to be the head coach of a franchise one day," Sciver-Brunt, 41, told Sky Sports.

"But I think being a mum, a working mum, the guilt is there. I feel guilty now, thinking about how he's being looked after, should I be doing that.

"I still have all that to figure out. It's more about letting go and managing that feeling, and knowing that a better me is a better mum to him."

Female head coaches are hard to come by in the women's game - particularly English ones.

Former captain Charlotte Edwards now leads England, having previously been with Southern Brave, so Australia's Lisa Keightley at MI London is the only one in this year's Hundred.

Although Sciver-Brunt said that she absolutely wants to progress her career further, she is also aware of how much she can realistically take on. With her wife playing for Rockets, at least parenting duties can be shared somewhat.

"I'm trying to make myself better, happier, and find my place in the world having once been a professional athlete," Sciver-Brunt added.

"I have a lot of passion for this, it's only been four days but I've loved it.

"I would love to do a couple of franchises, because a head coach role of a county just wouldn't fit - as soon as I do something, I want to do it to the best of my ability, almost too much!

"So I know I couldn't dive into that and do it all year round, because I've got to be a mum too. That's the goal - to give him the best life I can and to love him as much as I can, but I also want him to know who his mums were, and to enjoy this game too."

title: Senegal appeal date set after Afcon win overturned
description: The Court of Arbitration for Sport sets a date for a hearing over Senegal's appeal against being stripped of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations title.
fullText:
The Court of Arbitration for Sport has set a date for a hearing over Senegal's appeal against being stripped of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations title.

Hosts Morocco were declared the tournament winners after the Confederation of African Football (Caf) overturned the result of the final in January, which Senegal won 1-0.

The Senegalese players walked off the field after Morocco were awarded a stoppage-time penalty with the match goalless.

Following a delay of about 17 minutes, the players returned and Brahim Diaz's penalty was saved before Senegal's Pape Gueye scored an extra-time winner.

Senegal lodged their appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) on 25 March, seeking to set aside Caf's decision and reinstate them as tournament winners.

Caf deemed that Senegal had forfeited the final and awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory.

Caf and the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) did not agree to expedite the procedure so there will now be a hearing on 8 October.

According to a Cas statement, that follows the standard timeline.

Caf and the FRMF did not request that the hearing is made public so it will take place behind closed doors at the Cas headquarters in Lausanne, Switzerland.

Cas cannot state when a final decision will be announced but it will not be on the day of the hearing.

title: Phoenix all out for 64 as Hundred batting slump continues
description: The trend of low scores in The Hundred continues as Birmingham Phoenix suffer a nine-wicket defeat by Trent Rockets at Edgbaston.
fullText:
The Hundred women's competition, Edgbaston

Birmingham Phoenix 64 all out (95 balls): Perry 39 (33); Bates 3-10

Trent Rockets 68-1 (31 balls): Dunkley 43* (17); Filer 1-17

Birmingham Phoenix were bowled out for just 64 by Trent Rockets as the bowler-dominated start to The Hundred continued at Edgbaston.

Ellyse Perry played a lone hand with her 39 as no other Phoenix batter made it to double figures in a dire performance.

It was the joint second-lowest total in the Women's Hundred, and Phoenix also hold the record for the lowest when they were skittled for 54 against Northern Superchargers (now Sunrisers Leeds) in 2024.

Oval Invincibles (now MI London) also made 64 against Superchargers in the same year.

Debutant Samantha Bates - an uncapped Australian spinner - was the pick of Rockets' bowlers with 3-10 while seamer Georgia Elwiss took 3-13.

On another bowler-friendly surface, Australia's Kim Garth also bowled a miserly spell of 2-5 and leg-spinner Katie Levick took 1-8.

England batter Sophia Dunkley dominated the chase with 43 from 17 balls as it took Rockets just 31 balls to reach their target to complete a thoroughly one-sided contest.

It has been a struggle for batters in all four matches so far. London Spirit were bowled out for 80 in their first match on Thursday while the highest total has been Southern Brave's 126, which they successfully defended against Welsh Fire.

Rockets' only blemish was Ash Gardner's drop of Perry on nine, which would likely have resulted in even more humiliation for Phoenix as their captain was the only one to prove that the pitch was not a complete mystery.

It was a horror start to The Hundred for Phoenix which continues a difficult few years. Since 2023, they have finished bottom of the table and then seventh twice.

After the auction earlier this year, they strengthened their batting and though the conditions suited the bowlers and it was a good toss for Rockets to win, it was not a 64 all out pitch.

Davina Perrin - last year's breakout star - and Tammy Beaumont form the new opening partnership but Perrin was bowled by Elwiss for two off 10 balls and Beaumont chased a wide-ish delivery from Garth and was caught at point for a duck.

Those early wickets allowed Bates, a new name to The Hundred but with 139 matches to her name in Australia's WBBL, to settle into a nerveless spell.

Alice Capsey, another England player, was bowled missing an ambitious sweep, South Africa's Annerie Dercksen edged behind off a ball that did turn and Jemima Spence inexplicably tried a ramp and was caught at short fine leg.

Perry could only watch the chaos unfold at the other end as she desperately tried to revive the innings, whacking two fours and two sixes in her knock, but her team-mates had no answers to Rockets' consistency.

Dunkley, who has found herself in and out of England's T20 World Cup side, added further embarrassment to poor Phoenix as she made the pitch look like a road and clubbed eight fours and a six to start Rockets' campaign in style with a record-breaking chase in terms of fewest balls faced to complete vicotory.

title: IOC says Infantino complaint outside its scope
description: The IOC says it will not investigate Gianni Infantino as a complaint about the Fifa president is "outside" its scope.
fullText:
The International Olympic Committee says it will not investigate Gianni Infantino as a complaint about the Fifa president is outside its scope.

Human rights campaign group FairSquare complained to the IOC that Infantino had breached its charter by failing to adhere to rules on political neutrality "through statements or other clear expressions of support for the US president".

US President Donald Trump admitted during the World Cup that he had called Infantino to ask him to review a red card given to US striker Folarin Balogun.

The forward was expected to miss his side's last-16 tie against Belgium after being sent off during their 2-0 win over Bosnia-Herzegovina.

But, after the intervention from Trump the one-match ban was suspended for 12 months. No reason was given, beyond citing a rule that allows punishments to be suspended.

Balogun started the match, which Belgium won 4-1.

Infantino has been a member of the IOC since 2020.

Section two of the Olympic charter states: "Members of the IOC will not accept from governments, organisations, or other parties, any mandate or instructions liable to interfere with the freedom of their action and vote."

The IOC said the complaint against Infantino fell outside the jurisdiction of its ethics commission.

"The current complaint, with regard to the Fifa president, refers only to the international federation's decisions on its governance and its management, including its relations with government, and to the international federation's implementation of the rules of its sport, which are both outside the scope of application of the IOC code of ethics," it said.

The IOC statement came a day after it emerged the Norwegian Football Federation was considering filing a formal complaint to Fifa's ethics committee about the decision to suspend Balogun's automatic one-match ban.

In a statement provided to the BBC, NFF president Lise Klaveness said the federation had reacted with "strong concern" and a decision on whether or not to make a complaint would be made at its next board meeting.

The federation has already filed a complaint about Fifa's first Peace Prize being awarded to Trump.

Fifa has been contacted for comment.
